options.detail: A good coat, a regular hour, and a public-house. It is a short list. It is a long week.

quote.speaker: A barmaid in Pimlico
quote.text: He's a regular, sir, comes in Tuesdays and Fridays, and always meets the same gentleman. They never say a word to each other. They only swap hats.

success.outcome: It is the hats. On the second Friday you are in the next booth, with a newspaper, and you see a folded paper pass in the lining of a bowler. You say nothing, and follow the gentleman to a house in Kensington that has a look you recognise, the look of a place that belongs to the Professor. You do not go in. You go home, and write to your brother.

failure.outcome: The clerk has been told to be followed, or he has not, and either way he is very good at not being. You lose him twice in Whitehall and once in a hansom, and on the second Friday he does not come to the public-house at all. Mycroft receives your report with a politeness that is almost painful. 'Quite so,' he says. 'I had rather expected you would find that out.'

options.label: Pass It to Special Branch.
options.detail: A watching brief for professionals. It is slower, and it is surer, and it will not be yours.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Greaves
quote.text: I'll put two men on him, sir, and he'll never know. It will be a pleasure. We've been wanting somebody to look at that coat for a month.

options.outcome: Greaves takes it with the quiet delight of a man who has been waiting years to be given a thing to do. In ten days he has the clerk's whole week on a single sheet, and the clerk himself in a small bare room in Great Scotland Yard, explaining. You have not had to put a foot in Pimlico.

options.label: Report What You Know to Mycroft and Let Him Decide.
options.detail: He is the Government. If it is a matter for the Government, it is a matter for him.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You have done what I asked, Sherlock, and nothing at all that I did not. It is a very rare kind of obedience, and I do not know that I like it. But it is convenient.

options.outcome: Mycroft reads your note with his eyes shut, and files it in a drawer that locks with two keys. You never learn what became of the clerk. A fortnight later a better coat is seen on another man, in Whitehall, and nobody remarks on it.

FA.title: The Locked Room
FA.description: Tuesday 17 February. The sitting-room at 221B has not been so quiet since you were last ill. Mrs Hudson, who knows better than to knock, has left a tray on the landing and has gone away; the lamp is lit; the papers lie in heaps upon the carpet, and on the chair, and on the long deal table, with the weight of a winter's reading in them. You have told yourself a number of times that you are working alone because it is wiser, and that is what you are telling yourself now. You have, you realise, not spoken aloud for two days.

options.label: Take a Client's Case While You Think.
options.detail: A small matter, with a fee and a letter of thanks at the end of it. It will keep your name in the papers, and your mind from the wall.

quote.speaker: The scholar
quote.text: It was there on Tuesday, Mr Holmes, and on Wednesday it was not. We should be most grateful for any help at all.

options.outcome: You sort the notes on the mantelpiece, and choose, and put the rest in a drawer. It is an odd relief to be asked a question to which there is an answer.

options.label: Read the Papers Alone for a Week.
options.detail: Cuttings, ledgers, inquest reports. Every connexion on the wall, and no one to see it but you.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: He's not had a proper meal since Thursday, sir, and now he's asking me for the tobacco from the Persian slipper. I only say.

options.outcome: For seven days the room is blue with smoke and white with paper. When you open the curtains the pattern is plain upon the wall: a hundred small crimes, and one patient mind that has never been seen in any of them.

options.label: Plan the Road Out of England While You Still Have Time.
options.detail: A route, a disguise, a train, a passport in another name. A man who is going to have to run had better know how to.

quote.speaker: A travel agent
quote.text: Ah, Mr Henri Dubois? Yes, sir. Dover, Calais, and onward by the nine-forty. I should be glad to book it for any date you please, as long as you do not mind my not asking why.

options.outcome: You spend an afternoon in a dim office near Charing Cross, with a map and a pencil and a man who asks nothing at all. By evening you have a route written in your own cipher on the inside of a cigarette-case, and the odd, uneasy comfort of having made a decision you hope you will not need.

Y1.title: The Conference at the Yard
Y1.description: Saturday 25 April. The long room on the first floor of Scotland Yard smells of ink, wet wool and old tobacco. The Assistant Commissioner sits at the head of the table with his spectacles pushed up on his forehead, and eleven superintendents and inspectors sit down the sides, each with a sheet of paper bearing one address. You have been given twenty minutes. Lestrade has told them what you told him, and the faces round the table say plainly that they have heard a great many theories in their time and have rarely seen one end in anything but paperwork.

options.label: Present the Full Case: Statement, Ledger and Every Exhibit.
options.detail: Put it all on the table, in order, and let the evidence do the speaking.

quote.speaker: The Assistant Commissioner
quote.text: I have sat through a good many presentations, Mr Holmes. I have never before had one that ended with me asking how soon we could begin.

options.outcome: You speak for forty minutes. The Assistant Commissioner interrupts three times, each time to ask a more exact question, and the last time to ask for a pen. By noon the eleven warrants are drafted, the magistrates' clerks are summoned, and the long room has become the loudest place in London.

options.label: Ask for Only the Three Addresses You Can Prove, and Watch the Rest.
options.detail: A modest request, and an easy one to grant. It leaves eight houses unwatched.

quote.speaker: The Assistant Commissioner
quote.text: Three houses I can give you, Mr Holmes, and gladly. For the other eight, I should want rather more than an opinion.

options.outcome: He signs the order for three houses without a murmur, and says kind things about your caution. You take the paper. It is the safest thing that could have happened, and it is also the smallest.

options.label: Press for One Night, All Eleven, and Tell Nobody Below Inspector.
options.detail: A single stroke before they can warn one another. If anything leaks, it is all lost.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: It's a bold plan, Mr Holmes. It's what I'd do myself, if I were not afraid of what the Chief will say on Tuesday.

options.outcome: The room divides, and the Assistant Commissioner takes a long time to decide. In the end he sides with boldness, with a visible reluctance. The orders are drafted for Monday at first light. You are aware that from this moment your name is on every one of them.

options.label: Ask Lestrade for His Own Best Men at Every Door.
options.detail: The one inspector in the building who will vouch for you in front of his superiors. It spends a good deal of his credit.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll put my own name to it, Mr Holmes. I've said before that I'd stand behind you, and I'd as soon not be made a liar this late in the day. You'll have my best.

options.outcome: Lestrade rises in his place at the long table and says, in a flat plain voice, that he has known Mr Holmes for eleven years and has never known him wrong in a thing that mattered. It is not an eloquent speech. It is a very heavy one. The Assistant Commissioner, who has been looking at his watch, stops.
options.requiresHint: Needs Lestrade's trust

options.label: Win Over the Chief Inspector First.
options.detail: Lestrade has not said a word in your favour. The only man who can change that is the man above him.

quote.speaker: The Chief Inspector
quote.text: Mr Holmes, I will be plain. I have heard that you are unsteady. I will listen for ten minutes, and if I am not satisfied you will find that I am a very tedious man to persuade.

options.outcome: It takes forty minutes, and a good deal of patience, and you leave the Chief Inspector's room with a grudging nod and the beginnings of a reputation for being reasonable. Lestrade, in the corridor, does not look at you. But he opens the door.

echoes.text: The grey ledger lies in the middle of the table under a brass paperweight. Nobody likes to touch it.
Larch's statement, signed in a shorthand clerk's neat hand, is the first exhibit on the table.
On the corner of Lestrade's blotter is a card with a cabman's name on it. It has been there since February, and it has not once moved.

Y2.title: Warrants at Bow Street
Y2.description: Saturday afternoon. A warrant is a small thing, a sheet of paper and a signature, but without it every arrest on Monday is a kidnapping. The magistrate at Bow Street is a precise old gentleman with gouty feet, who reads each line twice and likes best to be asked in person. Lestrade's cab waits at the kerb. Behind you the Yard hums with the quiet energy of a great machine that has been told to start.

options.label: Go Yourself, in Your Best Coat, and Swear to the Facts.
options.detail: The magistrate trusts a man he can see. He will also take a very close look at you.

quote.speaker: The magistrate at Bow Street
quote.text: You say you saw this with your own eyes, Mr Holmes? Very good. You will understand that I shall ask you to say it twice.

success.outcome: You swear for an hour, and the old gentleman signs on the half-hour. The warrants go into Lestrade's coat in a bundle tied with green tape. There is a feeling in the cab on the way back that you have never quite felt before, of the machinery of the law moving on your word.

failure.outcome: The magistrate listens and nods and questions, and in the end he signs eight of the eleven. The three he refuses are the three that matter most: the Professor's own house, his bank, and the coaching establishment. 'Bring me the ledger,' he says kindly, 'and we shall see.'

options.label: Let Lestrade Swear Them. You Wait in the Corridor.
options.detail: He is a policeman with a clean record. You are a gentleman with a reputation for theories.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: It'll go better if it's me, Mr Holmes. No offence meant. The old man likes a uniform.

options.outcome: You sit on a bench under a portrait of a dead magistrate and smoke your pipe in defiance of a notice. Forty minutes later Lestrade comes out with a bundle of papers under his arm. Some are signed. Some, he says cheerfully, are signed in pencil, to be inked on Monday.

options.label: Skip Bow Street and Take a Home Office Minute From Mycroft.
options.detail: A paper from Whitehall will open every door at once. It will also be remembered.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I shall write you something that no magistrate will refuse. I shall also note, in a small private ledger of my own, that you owe me one.

options.outcome: The minute arrives by messenger within the hour, on thick paper with a Whitehall watermark. It is irregular, it is entirely effective, and it commits you to something you have not yet been asked to do. Lestrade does not like it, and says so. But he uses it.

options.label: Let Lestrade Vouch for You.
options.detail: A word from a man the Yard respects. He can do it once. It will mend a good deal, and it will use up what he had.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll say it to the Chief myself, Mr Holmes. I'll say I've known you eleven years. It'll cost me something. I'd as soon you didn't ask what.

options.outcome: Lestrade is gone an hour, and comes back with his collar undone and his hat in his hand. The Chief has agreed, he says, to take another look. The word goes round the building by noon. Doors that were closed are, for the moment, unlocked.

Y3.title: A Name in the Corridor
Y3.description: Sunday 26 April. Lestrade comes to Baker Street at seven in the morning, grey in the face, and shuts the door behind him. Somebody in the Yard is talking. Two of the eleven addresses were visited last night by a man in a good coat who was not an inspector, and both houses were found empty in the morning, with the fires still warm. He has narrowed it to a sergeant of long service, a man called Pike, who has a daughter at a fashionable school and a sick wife. There are twenty-two hours to the raid, and every one of them is a risk.

options.label: Expose Him at Once, Before the Whole Yard.
options.detail: The honest course, and the loudest. A traitor named is a traitor stopped, but a Yard in uproar is not a Yard that can act.

quote.speaker: Sergeant Pike
quote.text: It was for my wife, Mr Holmes. They said they would pay the doctors. I never told them more than I had to.

options.outcome: Pike is arrested in the Yard's own corridor, with half the building looking on. He weeps, and then is silent, and then gives up three more names in a flat voice that makes your skin crawl. The raid is safe. The Yard will take a month to recover its self-respect, and it will not forget who started it.

options.label: Feed Him a False List of Addresses and See Who Comes to Meet It.
options.detail: Turn the leak into a lantern. If it works, you will know the Professor's mind. If it fails, you will have told him your own.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: It's a risky game, Mr Holmes. If he suspects, we've given him the whole thing on a plate. But if he doesn't, we'll know the name of every man who hurries to the Professor's door.

success.outcome: Pike takes the bait, and the false list goes out to a Mayfair letter-box before supper. By midnight Wiggins's cousins, or Lestrade's constables, or both, have seen four men come to that box in turn, and three of them are names you did not have. The trap has caught more than the mouse.

failure.outcome: Pike does not take the bait; he takes the list straight to the Professor's man, and with it an exact account of how it came into his hands. The real addresses are changed by morning. You have not caught a spy. You have proved to the enemy that you know of him.

options.label: Tell Only Lestrade, and Move the Raid an Hour Earlier.
options.detail: Say nothing, trust no one, and shift the clock. A leak is only a danger if it has time to run.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: An hour won't kill us, Mr Holmes. And it'll be an hour that nobody in this building can have told him about. I'll see to the clocks myself.

options.outcome: Lestrade rewrites the order of march in his own hand, with his own pen, and carries it in his breast pocket until the morning. The leak goes uncaught, but it is outrun. You sleep poorly, aware of what an hour can contain.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of a man who has been looked after.

echoes.text: The warrants are in Lestrade's inside pocket, tied in green tape, and he pats them at every corner like a man checking for his watch.

Y4.title: The Last Night in London
Y4.description: Sunday evening. The fog has come up from the river, and Baker Street is wrapped in it like a parcel. From the sitting-room window you can see the lamp on the corner, a smear of yellow in a grey wall, and the shapes of the men who loiter beneath it. You are being watched. You are, in a curious way, glad of it. It means that on this last night he is still afraid of you. Mrs Hudson has banked the fire and gone to bed. The raids begin at four.

options.label: Sit Up With Lestrade and Go Over Each Address Again.
options.detail: Every door, every back stair, every cellar. A plan is only as good as its last re-reading.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: There's a coal-hole on the Kentish Town house that isn't on any plan, Mr Holmes. I found it myself in 'sixty-eight. If we don't stop it, he's out through the cellar like a rat.

options.outcome: You work until two. Lestrade remembers coal-holes, side-doors and a cousin's cellar, and you remember every cab-rank for a mile around each house. By the time you finish, the plan has changed in nine small ways, and every one of them has a face and a name.

options.label: Sleep. You Will Need Your Head.
options.detail: Three hours of plain, dull rest. It is the best weapon you possess, and the one you most often leave in the cupboard.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: I've put a hot brick in your bed, sir, and I've told the boy not to knock till half-past three. You'll do nobody any good with your eyes shut standing up.

options.outcome: You sleep like a child. When Lestrade's knock comes in the dark you are awake at once, clear-headed and cold, and remembering with surprise that you had a tendency, once, to think a man could do without it.

options.label: Walk the Streets to See the Places Once More in the Dark.
options.detail: Houses are not what they are on paper. A man learns more in an hour's stroll than in a month of reports.

quote.speaker: A lamplighter
quote.text: You'll be wanting to keep to the walls, sir. There's a gentleman at the end of the street with an odd-shaped walking-stick, and he's not been walking with it.

success.outcome: You walk three miles in the fog and see what the paper would never show: the unlit window, the cart left in the wrong alley, the doorkeeper who sits where no doorkeeper sits. You are back in Baker Street by one with your notebook full and your coat wet.

failure.outcome: Something strikes the wall at your shoulder with a flat, soft crack, and a splinter of brick stings your cheek. There is no sound of a gun. There is only the shape of a tall man in a long coat, a hundred yards off, putting something under his arm and walking calmly away. You have met Colonel Moran, and he has missed on purpose.

echoes.text: Watson is not here. You did not ask him. The armchair on the other side of the hearth is empty and a little cold.
Somewhere in Mayfair a false list lies in a letter-box, and tonight you cannot tell whether you are the cat or the mouse.
A man with a long coat and a walking-stick that he does not lean on has been seen at the end of Baker Street twice in a week. Mrs Hudson thought he was a clergyman.

Y5.title: Monday, Before Dawn
Y5.description: Monday 27 April. Eleven addresses, eleven parties of police, and one clock. At three minutes to four the first of the hansoms leaves the Yard without lamps. You have a place in a cab, and a map, and a decision to make about where you shall be. You cannot be at all of them. At the Professor's own house there is the man himself, perhaps, and his papers. At the Docks, there is the money, and the warehouse where a year's counterfeits wait to be shipped. And at the Yard there is the telegraph, and the only chance of knowing how the night goes.

options.label: Lead the Raid on the Professor's Own House.
options.detail: The centre of the web. If he is anywhere, he is here.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'd sooner you came with me, Mr Holmes, and not just because I'm afraid of what you'd say if you weren't there. He's a clever one. He's laid more traps than the Tower.

success.outcome: The door gives at the third blow. The house is lit and warm and empty, and in the study a chess game has been left unfinished, black to move. You find his private papers in a drawer that was closed with a second lock, and the map of the whole network folded in four on his writing-desk. He has gone, and he has left it all.

failure.outcome: The first man through the door is struck down by a trip-wire and a falling beam, and the second is shot in the shoulder from the landing. By the time the house is cleared the study has been burned, the ash is cold, and the Professor's servant is leaning out of an attic window laughing. It is the first time you have seen how thorough he is.

options.label: Take the Warehouse at the Docks Where the Money Moves.
options.detail: A year's forgeries, boxed for shipping. The quiet money of the whole gang.

quote.speaker: A Thames Division sergeant
quote.text: We've three boats on the river and a cordon on the quay, sir. Nothing gets off that wharf but by swimming, and I'd say it was a cold morning for it.

options.outcome: The warehouse is a long, dark, smelling place, and the crates are stencilled with the names of honest firms. In a back room you find the engraver's plates and four tons of paper. Nine men are arrested, and not one of them is higher than a foreman. But the money has been stopped.

options.label: Hold the Yard's Telegraph and Direct All Eleven by Wire.
options.detail: Sit at the centre of the web, for once, and be the spider.

quote.speaker: The telegraph clerk
quote.text: Number six reports the house empty, sir. Number three reports resistance. Number nine has the door open and nobody home. Do you wish me to send to the Chief Inspector?

options.outcome: For three hours the instrument chatters in the quiet room, and you read the night as a general reads a battle: by what arrives, and by what does not. It is cold work, and it is exact. When the last message comes in, you know that the net is drawn, and that something has slipped through it.

echoes.text: A flat, soft crack in the fog, and a splinter of brick, still sits in your memory. Colonel Moran is somewhere in London this morning, and he is not at any of the eleven addresses.

Y6.title: The Empty Chair
Y6.description: Monday noon. The reports come in from all over London, and their sense is the same: arrests, arrests, arrests, and no Professor. Thirty-one prisoners have been taken. A forger, three bankers' clerks, a bishop's secretary, a retired Colonel of Marines, a lady pawnbroker, and a dozen men of whom the police say only that they have been known to them for twenty years. But in the Professor's study the chair behind the desk is pushed back a little from the table, as if its owner had risen a moment ago, politely, to leave.

options.label: Order the Ports and the Stations Watched.
options.detail: A man like that cannot leave England unseen. Not quite. Not for a week.

quote.speaker: The Assistant Commissioner
quote.text: I can give you the Channel ports and the main termini, Mr Holmes. I cannot give you every cab-rank and every fishing-smack in the Thames estuary.

options.outcome: A hundred and forty constables are moved to the railway stations before dark, and a coastguard cutter is sent down to the Nore. It is an enormous labour, and you are aware throughout that the man you are looking for would have thought of it three weeks ago.

options.label: Go Through the Professor's Study Yourself, Paper by Paper.
options.detail: A man leaves himself in what he has written, however careful he is.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: We've taken what we found, Mr Holmes. But if there's something more in that room, I should be obliged if you'd tell me what.

options.outcome: You work through the afternoon in the cold study with a lamp and a glass. There is nothing in the desk, but under the carpet by the fireplace you find a charred half-sheet bearing four initials and a date in May. It is not a great deal. It is the first sign you have seen of a man who is, after all, in a hurry.

options.label: Return to Baker Street. The Rest Is the Yard's.
options.detail: You have done what you came to do. The tidying belongs to those who can be thanked for it.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: You look quite done up, sir. I've put the kettle on, and there's a cold fowl from last night, and not a word shall pass my lips about it.

options.outcome: You walk home, in a cab and then on foot, and let the fog take you. It is the first quiet afternoon in four months. By evening you are in your chair with a violin across your knee, and the Yard is making its own history without you.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of a man who has been looked after.

echoes.text: The map of the network lies on the Yard's table, folded in four, with the chess game in its box beside it.
The Docks have been closed for the day. The river is full of police boats, and an unwelcome silence.
You read it from the wire: eleven raids, ten successes, and one empty chair.

Y7.title: The Trial Season
Y7.description: Monday 8 June, the Central Criminal Court. The great dock at the Old Bailey holds thirty-one prisoners in a long grey row, and the gallery is packed to the doors. The Crown has chosen to try the lieutenants first, on the theory that the principal will follow. The defence has hired the most expensive counsel in London, a smooth, dry man with a gift for the single devastating question. You are in the witness box. The first thing he says is 'Mr Holmes, you are, I believe, a gentleman who is paid by the clue?'

options.label: Give Your Evidence Plainly and Hold to What You Can Prove.
options.detail: No theories, no dramatics. Say what you saw and nothing else, and let the jury do the thinking.

quote.speaker: Defence counsel
quote.text: You tell the jury, Mr Holmes, that a man's hat betrays his habits. Does the hat of the prisoner here betray his guilt? Pray be precise.

success.outcome: You answer for six hours, and not once do you embellish. By the third hour the jury has stopped looking at the counsel and has begun to look at you. When the judge sums up, he uses the words 'a witness of unusual exactitude.' The verdicts come in at dusk. Twenty-eight are guilty.

failure.outcome: The counsel is cleverer than you and better rested. He gets you to admit that you cannot prove the first link in your chain, and that you have never met the man who is supposed to be at the head of it. The jury goes out on a Friday and does not come back until Monday. Eleven of the prisoners are acquitted.

options.label: Put the Grey Ledger in Evidence and Let It Speak.
options.detail: The Professor's own handwriting, a hundred pages of it. There is no better witness and no more dangerous exhibit.

quote.speaker: Defence counsel
quote.text: My lord, I put it to the jury that this book was obtained by a burglary. I shall ask them to consider what manner of men are ready to break the law in the name of the law.

success.outcome: The cipher is read aloud, page by page, by a professor of mathematics from Cambridge who has never heard of the accused. Each entry he reads is checked against a bank-book, a bill, or a living witness. By the end of the second day the ledger has hanged more men than all the witnesses put together.

failure.outcome: The judge allows the book, but he rules the manner of its obtaining 'regrettable', and the jury has heard the word. Counsel makes it ring. 'The prosecution's best witness,' he says, 'is a stolen book.' It does not decide the case, but it is a stain upon it, and upon you.

options.label: Let Lestrade Carry the Case. Keep Your Name Off the Record.
options.detail: You have a reputation for theory, and the Crown has a reputation for dullness. Perhaps dullness will serve.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: If it's all the same to you, Mr Holmes, I'll tell it my own way. It won't be as good, but it'll be steady.

options.outcome: Lestrade carries the case with the patience of an ox, and the Crown wins eighteen convictions to thirteen acquittals. It is a plain victory, and a limited one. You sit in the gallery in a plain coat and do not give your name to the newspapers.

options.label: Let Lestrade Vouch for You.
options.detail: A word from a man the Yard respects. He can do it once. It will mend a good deal, and it will use up what he had.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll say it to the Chief myself, Mr Holmes. I'll say I've known you eleven years. It'll cost me something. I'd as soon you didn't ask what.

options.outcome: Lestrade is gone an hour, and comes back with his collar undone and his hat in his hand. The Chief has agreed, he says, to take another look. The word goes round the building by noon. Doors that were closed are, for the moment, unlocked.

echoes.text: Counsel for the defence has a question about a certain night in the Marylebone Road. He has had it ready for weeks.
Among the letters on the Crown's table is one from the governors of the Clerkenwell Institute, speaking warmly of your character.
Counsel's question about the Marylebone Road falls flat. The divisional book has no such entry, because you went to the Superintendent yourself, and he burned the page.

Y8.title: A Visitor From Whitehall
Y8.description: Wednesday 10 June. The visitor comes in a hansom without a number, which is the first thing you notice, and he climbs the seventeen steps with the slow, laboured dignity of a man who dislikes every one of them. Mycroft Holmes has not been in Baker Street for two years. He sits in your chair, unasked, takes off his gloves, and tells you in an even voice that the Professor's papers, which have been in Government hands since Tuesday, contain the names of six members of the House of Commons, two of the Lords, and a bishop. The Government would very much prefer that these names remain in a locked room.

options.label: Refuse. The Law Is the Law.
options.detail: A man who sells justice by the pound is no better than the man he catches. You will not oblige him.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are the only man in England I could not frighten, Sherlock, and I confess it is the quality I like least in you.

options.outcome: Mycroft says nothing for a long while. Then he rises, puts on his gloves, and goes down the seventeen steps with the grim step of a man who has just lost a game he did not know he was playing. At the door he turns and says, quite gently, 'I hope you know what you have done.' You do. You are not sorry.

options.label: Accept a Closed Hearing and the Professor's Silence.
options.detail: A sealed trial, a guaranteed verdict, and a gag upon every name. It is not justice. It is an arrangement.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: The principle is this: nothing will ever be said in public that cannot be said in front of a bishop. The practice is a good deal less elevated. I shall make the arrangements.

options.outcome: Mycroft is delighted, and does not show it. The meeting is brief. When he has gone you find on the mantelpiece, under the clock, a small envelope bearing the Government's seal, a sum of money, and a short note. 'For services.' You put it in the fire.

options.label: Ask What He Is Afraid Of.
options.detail: A man like Mycroft is never merely afraid. He is afraid of something specific, and it would help to know what.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I am afraid, Sherlock, that the Professor's ledger contains a list of men who do not know that they are in it. And that the list is considerably longer than the one I carry in my head.

options.outcome: He tells you more than he meant to, which is, for Mycroft, a form of respect. The Professor kept a second ledger, and a second set of secrets, and a hand in the Government itself. You thank him. When he has gone you sit for an hour in the dark, adding up the names.

echoes.text: He reminds you, with the lightest of smiles, that a certain Home Office minute was not a free gift.

Y2B.title: The Press at the Door
Y2B.description: Saturday evening. A reporter has been loitering in the corridor outside the long room since four, a plump, eager young man named Alderson from the Standard, with a pencil behind his ear and a hat that has seen a great many doors. He knows that something is afoot. He knows it as a dog knows a storm. Eleven warrants, forty constables and a Chief Inspector who has not been seen to smile in two days are hard to hide from a man whose living is made by asking. If a single word reaches the Professor's friends before Monday, the net is empty.

options.label: Give Him a Statement That Says Nothing at Great Length.
options.detail: Courteous, vague and dull. The oldest trick in the Yard, and the one that most often works.

quote.speaker: Mr Alderson of the Standard
quote.text: Very good, Mr Holmes. 'Inquiries are proceeding in several quarters.' I shall write it down. I shall also write, if you don't mind, that you looked remarkably cheerful.

options.outcome: He takes it down with a patient smile, and goes away with the air of a man who has been given a very large and very empty parcel. The statement appears on Monday in four lines, on page six, under the shipping news. Nobody reads it. You have done what you set out to do.

options.label: Promise Him an Exclusive on Monday Night, in Return for Silence Until Then.
options.detail: A reporter with a promise is a reporter with a reason to keep quiet. It will make you a friend in the press, and a debtor.

quote.speaker: Mr Alderson of the Standard
quote.text: Monday night, Mr Holmes, and the whole story, from the first word? You have my honour, and my editor's, which is worth a good deal less. I shall be as dumb as a stone.

options.outcome: He is as good as his word. He is also, you reflect, the first newspaper man in London who has been told the date of a raid, and the knowledge sits in your stomach like a cold stone. But the editor has a Chief Inspector of his own, and nobody tells the Professor. On Monday evening you give him the whole of it, and he writes it beautifully.

options.label: Have Lestrade Mislay Him in the Building.
options.detail: A staircase, a locked door, a long wait. It is not very honest. It will, however, keep him until Tuesday.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I don't like it, Mr Holmes. A man's a man, even if he writes for the papers. But I suppose he'll thank us for the sleep. I'll put him in the records room with a pot of tea.

options.outcome: Alderson is invited, with every civility, to look at a very rare set of ledgers in the records room, and is somehow forgotten. He sits among the dust and the files until Tuesday morning. He is furious, and he writes a short, sour piece about the Yard's hospitality, and you learn that a man who is locked up for a good cause can still hold a grudge.

options.label: Sell the Story to the Standard's Rival for a Handsome Sum.
options.detail: A rival paper will pay ten pounds for a few lines of nonsense. It will not hurt the raid. It will hurt your name.

quote.speaker: A sub-editor of the Evening Mail
quote.text: Ten pounds, Mr Holmes, for the three paragraphs and a signature? I am sure the proprietor would call it cheap. He would call it very cheap indeed.

options.outcome: You take the ten pounds and write three paragraphs of agreeable fiction, and the sub-editor pays without reading them. It is the sort of expedient that a gentleman with money does not need, and a gentleman without it learns about at a stroke. By Tuesday the Standard is cold to you, and the Yard has noticed.

Y5B.title: The Prisoners' Corridor
Y5B.description: Monday afternoon, a long, low corridor beneath the Yard, smelling of wet stone and carbolic. Thirty-one prisoners have been brought in from eleven addresses, and they sit in a row of cells with their coats over their knees and the stunned, affronted faces of people who have never in their lives been told what to do. Lestrade has a list. Three of the names on it are worth your afternoon: the bishop's secretary, a mild, grey, scrupulous man named Lyle; a lady pawnbroker in Lambeth called Mrs Venn; and a retired Colonel of Marines who is shouting for a lawyer. You have time to speak to one.

options.label: Speak to the Bishop's Secretary.
options.detail: A frightened, orderly man who has been doing what he was told for years and has never once asked why. He will break at a touch.

quote.speaker: Mr Lyle
quote.text: I thought it was the diocese, Mr Holmes. They told me it was a matter of church investments. I never thought to ask which church.

options.outcome: He weeps, quietly and neatly, into a folded handkerchief, and gives you everything: the names of nine clients, a code for the invoices, and the shape of the Professor's arrangement with the cab-yards. It is a long, gentle confession. At the end of it he asks whether the Bishop will be told. You do not know what to say.

options.label: Speak to Mrs Venn, the Lambeth Pawnbroker.
options.detail: A hard, quick, shrewd woman with a head for figures and no illusions. If she talks, it will be worth a month. If she doesn't, she will have taught you something.

quote.speaker: Mrs Venn
quote.text: You may ask me what you please, Mr Holmes. I shall answer what I please. I've kept a shop in Lambeth for thirty years, and I never yet gave a policeman more than the time.

success.outcome: She talks, in the end, for the plain reason that you have understood her arithmetic. Every pawn-ticket in her shop was a loan against a name, and every name was a line in the Professor's ledger. She gives you the key to the cipher, and a drawer's worth of tickets, with the air of a woman who has decided that she would rather be an honest witness than a poor prisoner.

failure.outcome: She says nothing at all, for forty minutes, with an unwavering and almost cheerful composure. At the end she asks whether you have a daughter. You have not. She remarks that it is a pity, and asks for her tea. You come out of the cell with nothing but the knowledge that she is the better detective.

options.label: Leave the Questioning to Lestrade and Go Home to Think.
options.detail: Policemen question prisoners. A detective's work is to see what the questions mean.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll do it properly, Mr Holmes. I'll do it slowly, and I'll do it by the book. We'll have the whole lot of them by Friday, you wait and see.

options.outcome: You leave the Colonel to be shouted down by the Yard, and the pawnbroker to be outwaited, and the bishop's secretary to be treated with a kindness that you can hear through the wall. It is a sensible division of labour. You go home and sleep, and wake to find that three of the prisoners have talked and four have been bailed, and that nothing at all has changed.

YX1.title: The Professor's Study
YX1.description: Monday, three in the afternoon. The study is warm still, as though the man who sat in it had just walked out, and everything in it has the look of a room arranged to be looked at. A chess game stands unfinished on a table by the window, black to move, with the pieces in an elaborate and rather beautiful position. The carpet below the desk is worn in a long crescent, as if someone had pushed a heavy chair back and forth upon it a great many times. And on the far wall, where the books are ranged in tidy ranks, there is a single gap about the width of a thumb.

options.label: Study the Unfinished Chess Game.
options.detail: A game left mid-play is a message of a kind. It may tell you where the Professor intends to go.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: He's an excellent player, they say, Mr Holmes. Beat the Chief Inspector in nine moves at a Christmas party, and apologised for taking so long.

options.outcome: You study the position for twenty minutes, and the more you study it the more beautiful it becomes. It is a composed problem, white to mate in four, and it has nothing at all to do with the matter. It is the work of a man who likes to be looked at, and wished you to look.

options.label: Crouch by the Desk and Study the Worn Crescent in the Carpet.
options.detail: A carpet is a map of habit. A man does not wear a crescent without a reason.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: It's only a worn patch, Mr Holmes. We've found them in every room in London where a man's kept a chair. I don't see what you can learn from it.

options.outcome: The crescent is not made by a chair. It is made by a panel in the wainscot that swings outward, a hand's breadth at a time, and is hinged to the wall behind the desk. The panel is shut and papered over, but the dust along its edge has been disturbed within the week. The room has a second door, and it leads next door.

options.label: Look at the Gap in the Bookshelf.
options.detail: A missing book is a statement, if a man troubles to read it. It is not usually a clever man's mistake.

quote.speaker: The constable at the door
quote.text: They're all in order, sir. They're alphabetical. Whoever's taken one has been very careful to put the others back straight.

options.outcome: The gap sits between a volume of Euler and a volume of Gauss. The dust on the shelf is thick on either side and thin in the middle, so the book was taken recently, and by a man who put the others straight. You cannot tell what it was. You spend a long time looking at the space, which is not unlike looking at a tooth that has been drawn.

YX2.title: The Desk and the Shelf
YX2.description: Monday, four o'clock. The light is going out of the room, and with it the first confidence of the afternoon. The desk has three drawers, and the Yard has been through them already. The fireplace holds the ashes of a very large number of papers. The shelves, on the far wall, stand in their ranks like an audience. You have time to look properly at one more thing before the dark comes, and the lamp must be lit.

options.label: Go Through the Desk Drawers Again.
options.detail: The Yard has done it once. A second reading, by a man who knows what to look for, is a different thing.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: We've been through them, Mr Holmes. Every one of them. There's nothing but pens and paper and a very old bottle of ink.

options.outcome: There is nothing but pens and paper and a very old bottle of ink. The drawers were emptied some time before you came, and neatly, with the wooden bottoms polished. It is the work of a man who knew he might be visited, and has taken the trouble to show you that he is not ashamed.

options.label: Find What the Missing Book Was.
options.detail: A book left a gap, and the gap left a shape. It was not a large book. It was a thin one, with a limp cover, and it had been handled a great deal.

quote.speaker: The Professor's housekeeper
quote.text: That was Mr Bradshaw's, sir, the railway book. The Professor looked at it every night. He had the corner turned down. I think it was a page about Hackney, but I can't swear to it.

options.outcome: The housekeeper, a trembling woman of sixty who has been in the house six years and has never been asked a question, remembers the book at once. It was a Bradshaw, the thin red-covered kind, and the page at the corner was turned down for the line to Hackney. It was taken on Friday. The Professor has not been to Hackney in six years, and he is going there now.

options.label: Sift the Ashes in the Grate.
options.detail: A fire that burned a great many papers burned some of them badly. A scrap, a corner, a watermark.

quote.speaker: The constable at the door
quote.text: We had those out on a tray at noon, sir. They're a mess, I'm afraid. There wasn't a whole sheet in the lot.

options.outcome: You work through them with a pair of tweezers and a lens, sheet by blackened sheet. They are what the constable said they were: a mess. You find a corner with three letters and half a date, and the broken edge of a cipher. It is very little. It is, you think, exactly as much as the Professor intended you to find.

YX3.title: The Deduction in the Study
YX3.description: Monday, six o'clock. The lamp is lit, and the Chief Inspector has come in with his hat still on, and Lestrade stands in the doorway with his arms folded. They want to know where the Professor has gone. You have the traces laid out in a row on the writing-table, and you are very tired, and you are, for the first time since January, a little afraid that you have missed the obvious. It is, in the end, a question of what you saw, and what you were willing to see.

options.label: Name His Road: Through the Party Wall, Then by Canal to Hackney.
options.detail: The carpet and the missing guide, together. He did not leave by the front. He left by the back of the house next door, and he is bound for a house in Hackney.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Through the next house? It never occurred to me, Mr Holmes. I'd have sworn the wall was solid. Give me a man with a mallet and I'll tell you in ten minutes.

options.outcome: Lestrade's man with a mallet takes eight minutes, and the panel is exactly where you said it would be. The next house has a gate to a lane, and the lane has a mark of wheels. The Professor has been in Hackney for two days. It is a very small piece of the puzzle, and for the first time since January the whole of it seems to lean in your direction.
options.requiresHint: Needs both traces: the worn carpet and the missing guide

options.label: Venture That He Has Gone to Hackney, and Say No More.
options.detail: A single trace and a single guess. It will do some good, and will leave the details to chance.

quote.speaker: The Chief Inspector
quote.text: Hackney is a very big place, Mr Holmes. I could put every man I have into it and still miss him. But I take it as a lead, and I shall use it as one.

options.outcome: You say that you believe the Professor has gone east, and you say why, and the Chief Inspector nods slowly and writes it on the back of an envelope. It is not much. It is more than he had before, and rather less than you would have liked. The Yard puts a watch on the eastern railway stations, and waits.
options.requiresHint: Needs one of the two traces

options.label: Admit You Have Not Read the Room.
options.detail: A confession of a kind. The Chief Inspector will not enjoy it. It will, at least, be true.

quote.speaker: The Chief Inspector
quote.text: I had hoped for something, Mr Holmes. It is not a thing I say lightly. But it is as well to be told, plainly, that the great detective has nothing to tell us.

options.outcome: You tell him the truth, and the truth is received with a silence of the kind that has an edge to it. The Chief Inspector thanks you with great civility. Lestrade, in the doorway, looks at his boots. You walk home alone through the wet streets, and for the first time you are not at all sure whether you are the cleverest man in London, or merely the most tired.

Y7B.title: The Witness for the Crown
Y7B.description: Tuesday 9 June, the evening before the Crown calls its principal witness. The Crown has one: a single, fragile, indispensable person whose account ties the whole ledger to the whole gang. It is a scared man or a grieving woman, depending on how the spring has gone, and in either case a person who has come a long way to say a hard thing in a public room. The defence will try to break them in an hour. The Crown's counsel is a decent, dry man, with no instinct whatever for the human being at the centre of his case.

options.label: Sit With the Witness Through the Night.
options.detail: Talk, or say nothing, as they prefer. A frightened person is steadier for being kept company.

quote.speaker: The witness
quote.text: I had not thought it would be so hard to say it aloud. It was easier in my head. I should be glad if you would stay, Mr Holmes, even if neither of us talks.

options.outcome: You sit by the fire until the church clocks strike four, saying little. In the morning the witness gives evidence in a clear, level voice that surprises everybody in the court, including, you suspect, the witness. You are not sure that you had much to do with it. But it is the kind of thing that you would rather have done than not.

options.label: Rehearse a Hostile Cross-Examination With Lestrade Playing Counsel.
options.detail: Hard questions, put roughly, in an empty room. It is a rough way to prepare a witness, and a good one.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I do not like to be so unkind, Mr Holmes. But if I'm to be the defence counsel, then I'll do it properly. Now, sir, isn't it true that you were paid for this evidence?

options.outcome: Lestrade is surprisingly good at it, and the witness, at the end of a gruelling hour, is surprisingly steady. In the courtroom the next day the real counsel puts the same question in almost the same words, and the answer comes back, calm and clean, as if by habit. It is the most useful evening you have ever spent in a police station.

options.label: Leave It to the Crown's Counsel.
options.detail: It is his case. A detective who interferes with a witness is a detective who can be accused of coaching one.

quote.speaker: The Crown's counsel
quote.text: Thank you, Mr Holmes, but I have always found it best to let a witness tell the truth in his own way. The jury sees the difference. It always does.

options.outcome: You stay away, and the counsel conducts his case with scrupulous propriety. The witness gives evidence in a voice that trembles at every second sentence, and the defence takes it in pieces with a patient and shining skill. The case survives. It does not survive with any glory.

echoes.text: The witness is Tobias Larch. He has grown a little in the months since March, and he sits with his hands folded as if afraid of dropping them.
The witness is Miss Larch, in black, with her brother's letters in her bag. She asked, as a favour, to be allowed to be the one.

Y9.title: The House in Hackney
Y9.description: Friday 19 June, midnight. The house is a plain, flat-faced villa at the end of a back street, with a lane at one side and a canal at the back, and a lamp in the upper window that has been burning since Tuesday. Lestrade has twenty men and a dark lantern. You have a map, a watch, and a very clear sense that the whole of the work since January comes down to what you do in the next three hours. The Professor, if he is inside, will not leave by a door he thinks is watched. The question is which door he thinks is not.

options.label: Put Lestrade's Best Men on Both the Lane and the Canal.
options.detail: Cover every exit and trust no one. It is thorough, slow and exactly what a clever man would have expected.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Ten at the lane and ten at the canal, Mr Holmes, and a man on the roof of the corn-chandler's with a dark lantern. If he's in there, he'll have to sprout wings.

options.outcome: Lestrade posts the men with a precision that does him credit. The lane is held by a sergeant and eight men, and the canal by a dozen with a boat. For two hours nothing moves in the villa but the lamp. It is a net with every knot tied. You cannot rid yourself of the thought that a spider does not weave a web without a way out of it.

options.label: Put Wiggins's Boys on the Rooftops and the Towpath.
options.detail: Twelve small shadows on twelve slates, who can see further than a constable and be seen by no one.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: We'll have every roof from here to the gasworks, Mr Holmes. If he as much as puts his nose out of a chimney, there'll be twelve boys know it before he's got his hat on.

options.outcome: The boys go up like a flight of starlings, and at one in the morning you cannot see one of them. Their reports come down by a string of whistles from slate to slate: a lamp lit, a lamp put out, a cab at the end of the street with its horse in a nosebag. It is a quieter net than Lestrade's, and a finer one.

options.label: Trust Your Reading of the Study and Watch the Canal Alone.
options.detail: If you read the room correctly, he will leave by the back of the house and take a boat. If you did not, you will have let him walk out of the front.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: You're quite sure, Mr Holmes? I'll tell you plainly, if you're wrong, I've half my men standing round a house with nothing in it. But I've never known you wrong about a floor.

options.outcome: Lestrade moves his men to the canal in the dark, with the grim face of a man placing his whole stake on a single card. The lane is left to a single constable with a whistle. You stand on the towpath in the cold and watch the water. It is the boldest stroke of the campaign, and you know, as you wait, exactly how foolish it will look if the Professor does not come.
options.requiresHint: Needs your reading of the Professor's study

options.label: Have Lestrade Hold the Lane Himself.
options.detail: A man you can trust at the door, with the lantern and the whistle. It is the one watch you will not have to check.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Leave the lane to me, Mr Holmes. I'll be at the door myself, with the dark lantern, and nobody will come out of it that I haven't had a look at first.

options.outcome: Lestrade takes the lane in person, in his old coat, with the lantern shuttered and his whistle in his teeth. You turn to the canal knowing that behind you there is a policeman of twenty years' standing who will stand there till the sun comes up. It is the most restful thing that has happened tonight.
options.requiresHint: Needs Lestrade's trust

echoes.text: In a cab at the end of the street, with the blinds drawn, a plump young man with a pencil is waiting for his exclusive. You have not told him which house.
The boys are already on the roofs.
Somewhere in the dark there is a soft metallic click, like a brass catch, that might be a latch or might not.

Y9B.title: The Cab at the Corner
Y9B.description: Saturday 20 June, two in the morning. A single lamp comes on in the lower window, and goes out. A moment later a cab, which has been standing in the next street with its horse in a nosebag, begins very quietly to move. Nobody has been seen to enter it. Nobody has been seen to leave the house. But something has shifted in the dark, in the way a cat shifts on a chair, and you know, with a sudden dry certainty, that the Professor is not in the villa. He is in that cab, and the cab is turning the corner towards the Cambridge Road.

options.label: Block the Cab at the Junction With Lestrade's Van.
options.detail: A heavy vehicle across the road, at a speed the Professor cannot out-run. It is crude, and it can be done.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: The van's round the corner, Mr Holmes. If you can get him to the junction before he sees it, we'll have him like a rabbit in a gate.

success.outcome: The van swings out of the dark across the Cambridge Road, a heavy, ugly, unanswerable bulk of a thing, and the cab pulls up with a scream of iron. The driver puts up his hands. Inside, a tall figure sits very still, with a hat on his knee, and does not so much as lift his head. He has, you reflect, never been in a position he could not think his way out of before.

failure.outcome: The van is late by a few seconds. The cab goes through the junction at a gallop, and the last you see of it is a tail-lamp bobbing east towards Stratford. Lestrade swears gently, and with feeling. You have lost the best chance of the night, and the Professor has not so much as raised his voice.

options.label: Follow in a Hansom With the Bishop's Secretary's Knowledge of the Cab-Yards.
options.detail: A man who knows which cab-yard a particular cab belongs to knows where it will be at dawn.

quote.speaker: Mr Lyle
quote.text: It is the Poplar yard's number nine, sir, a bay with a white blaze. It takes the Professor to Limehouse every Saturday at three and waits an hour. I only ever saw the horse.

options.outcome: You do not chase the cab. You walk to the Poplar yard, with Lestrade and four men, and wait in the stable beside a bay horse with a white blaze. At a quarter to three the cab comes in, and the Professor steps down in the lamplight. He looks at you for a very long moment, and then, almost with relief, at the hands of the constable who has taken him by the arm.
options.requiresHint: Needs a prisoner's knowledge of the cab-yards

options.label: Wire Every Railway Station East of the City.
options.detail: A tedious and indirect measure. It will not catch the cab. It may catch the man, if he is so incautious as to take a train.

quote.speaker: The telegraph clerk
quote.text: Forty-one stations, sir, and I've only the one instrument. I shall send them in order of the likeliest. I don't promise they'll all be read before breakfast.

options.outcome: For two hours the telegraph at the Yard rattles in the quiet building, and a hundred sleepy station-masters are woken to look at a description. The Professor does not take a train. He takes a boat, a barge, and a cart, and by dawn he is in a place where there is no telegraph at all. It was never going to work, and you have the dull satisfaction of having tried.

echoes.text: Somewhere above you a very small whistle passes from slate to slate. The boys have seen it too.

Y9C.title: The Towpath
Y9C.description: Saturday, three in the morning. The cold is very great, and the canal is as black and still as a sheet of iron. Whatever you did in the last two hours, the end of it comes down to this: a lamp-post, a stretch of towpath, and the long, patient figure of a man who has just discovered that for the first time in ten years he has been outplayed, or very nearly. If the net is complete he will walk into it. If it has a gap he will walk through. Lestrade stands at your elbow, breathing quietly, with his handcuffs in his hand.

options.label: Take Him Now. The Net Is Complete.
options.detail: Every door covered, the cab stopped. There is no gap in it. Say the word, and he is yours.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Professor Moriarty, I arrest you on a charge of conspiracy. It is, as it happens, only the first of a good many, and I should advise you to say nothing at all.

options.outcome: The Professor lowers his hat with extraordinary slowness. He looks at you, and at Lestrade, and at the twelve men on the towpath, and at the black water, and then he smiles, a thin, interested smile, as at a problem that has been correctly stated. 'I congratulate you, Mr Holmes,' he says. 'I had not thought it possible.' He holds out his wrists.
options.requiresHint: Needs the watch set and the cab stopped

options.label: Close the Net and Trust the Odds.
options.detail: Whatever you have missed, take your chance. A gap in the net is a gap, but it is not a certainty.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: It's now or never, Mr Holmes. If you're going to give the word, you had better give it quickly, because he's seen the lantern.

success.outcome: He does not run. A clever man does not run when he is not certain, and he is not certain. Lestrade's men close in, and the long figure goes, with great dignity, into the van. You are not at all sure, afterwards, how you did it. It was, as the Professor himself would say, an affair of probabilities.

failure.outcome: The gap was exactly where he thought it was. A shadow goes under the bridge, and a boat noses out of the reeds, and by the time Lestrade's whistle has finished sounding there is a long, black, quiet reach of water and nothing on it. The Professor has gone, again, as a thought goes.

options.label: Let the State Take Him.
options.detail: A single word to your brother, and the Professor will never be seen in a court. Nor, probably, in daylight.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You have chosen wisely, Sherlock. I know it is not what you would have chosen, if you had the choosing of it. But the world has a good many more of him than it has of you.

options.outcome: You send the word in a single line, and the answer comes back within the hour, in your brother's hand: one word, 'Noted.' A closed carriage is standing in the lane before the lamps are lit. You do not go down to look.

options.label: Close the File and Go Home.
options.detail: You have broken his gang. You have no more to give. Perhaps that is enough.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You have done a very great thing, Holmes. I think you had better stop doing it before it does something to you.

options.outcome: You leave the lamp burning on the towpath and the van standing in the lane, and you walk home. For the first time since January there is nothing at all in your pockets, and no appointment in your book.

echoes.text: You are standing at the canal and nowhere else. If you have read the study wrong, the whole of the night is lost.

S1.title: Wiggins's Map
S1.description: Saturday 25 April. The kitchen at 221B has not seen so many people since the Jubilee. Wiggins stands on a chair with a roll of brown wallpaper unrolled across the table, and eleven small, grave faces peer over the edge of it. The boys have drawn the Professor's London in coloured chalks: a counting-house in Shoreditch where the forged bills are made, a cab-yard in Kentish Town where Colonel Moran's men drill, a printer's shop in Clerkenwell that turns out the false letters, and a public-house in Wapping. On Monday the Yard will do what it can. You have chosen not to wait for it.

options.label: Hit the Money: The Counting-House in Shoreditch.
options.detail: Go in by night and take the plates and the paper. The law will not like how you got them.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: There's a boy goes in through the coal-chute every morning at six to light the stove. He'd let us in for a tanner, and think himself lucky.

options.outcome: The chute is narrow and black, and the stove is cold. By four in the morning you are out again with a satchel of engraved plates, a ream of watermarked paper and a ledger of foreign addresses. The lock on the front door has not been touched. The Professor's clerks will arrive at nine to find nothing out of place except the money.

options.label: Hit the Muscle: The Cab-Yard Where Moran's Men Drill.
options.detail: Scatter the Professor's rough work before it can be turned on you.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: They've got twelve men and eight horses, Mr Holmes, and a dog that bites. I can get the boys over the wall, but I can't get 'em back.

success.outcome: The boys go over the wall at midnight and the horses go out of the gate at one. By two the yard is full of confusion, and the Professor's men are swearing at each other in the road. You watch from a rooftop, and by dawn you have a list of eleven names and the weak spot of every one.

failure.outcome: The dog is not asleep, and the men are not drunk. Wiggins gets the boys over the wall again in a hurry, but not before one of the grooms has seen your face by the lantern. You spend the dawn in a cab with a torn sleeve and a bad conscience.

options.label: Hit the Paper: The Printer in Clerkenwell.
options.detail: The false letters are the soft belly of the whole business. Strike there and a hundred lies stop at once.

quote.speaker: The printer's apprentice
quote.text: He sets 'em up himself, sir, and burns the type after. But he never burns the proofs. They're in a tin under the bench.

options.outcome: A shilling and a long conversation with an apprentice in a leather apron gives you the tin. The proofs are in a dozen hands, and every one of them is a letter that has ruined somebody. You take them away quietly, without a quarrel, and leave the printer none the wiser.

echoes.text: You know a name, now: Fitch, who drives from a yard in Kentish Town. The yard is on Wiggins's map.
The cab-yard in Kentish Town is not a stranger to you. You have stood in its gateway, and you know which of its foremen has the shoulders of a prize-fighter.
The dog-cart with the yellow wheels is on the map in red chalk, with a small neat note: 'GREEN DOOR, CAMDEN TOWN'.
The Colonel's name is on the boys' map in a different colour, and a line under it, and a question mark.

S2.title: Disguise at the Docks
S2.description: Sunday 26 April, a raw dawn. The public-house in Wapping is called the Anchor and Hope, and it is the only place in London where the Professor's lieutenants meet without their hats off. A hundred yards of mud and rope divide you from its window. You have a sailor's jacket, a cap, a week's growth of beard, and the memory of a lifetime's study of how men walk when they are old and drunk and lost. You are a master of disguise, and you have never in your life been more afraid of being seen.

options.label: Go In Yourself as an Old Sailor.
options.detail: Sit in the snug with a pint and a pipe, and listen. It is a trade you know.

quote.speaker: The landlord
quote.text: Mind how you go, grandad. This isn't a house for old men who've lost their way.

success.outcome: For two hours you are a stooped old tar who has spent his last half-crown on rum. Three men at the next table speak of Monday and the Yard, and of a fourth man who is to be 'seen to' on the Thursday. You learn which road the Professor's carriage takes when it leaves the City, and which lamp-post he stops beside.

failure.outcome: One of the men at the next table has a long, thin scar across his cheek, and he looks at your hands. They are an old man's hands, in every line but one: the long, quick fingers of a violinist. You are out of the back door before he has finished his drink, and in the river before he has finished his thought.

options.label: Send Wiggins's Quickest Boy In With a Tray of Matches.
options.detail: A child selling matches is a piece of furniture. He may hear a great deal, and be thanked for none of it.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: Alf can do it, Mr Holmes. He's the nippiest. He's been in worse places than that, and he never once got caught.

options.outcome: Alf goes in at seven with a tray on a string around his neck, and comes out at nine with a stale bun and three overheard names. You pay him a shilling and watch him run home down the Highway, a small black shape against the lamps. You tell yourself that you would never send a child where you would not go.

options.label: Watch From a Rooftop With Field-Glasses.
options.detail: Cold, slow, and safe. You will see who comes and goes, but never what they say.

quote.speaker: A bargeman below
quote.text: You'll catch your death up there, mister. And I'll not have it said I didn't tell you.

options.outcome: You count thirty-one men through the door in seven hours, and note the hat, the walk and the watch-chain of every one of them. You catch a cold. You learn very little that a quicker man could not have told you in a quarter of an hour, but you do not put a hand wrong.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of a man who has been looked after.

S3.title: Moran at the Window
S3.description: Monday 27 April. At a quarter to nine in the evening, in the lamplit sitting-room, you reach out to turn the lamp and the glass of the window beside you shatters without a sound. There is a small round hole in the plaster of the opposite wall. No report, no flash, no echo. An air-gun, then, in the hands of a man who is the best heavy-game shot the Indian Army has ever produced. Colonel Sebastian Moran has begun to hunt you, and he does it as he has hunted tigers: patiently, from a high place, and without hurry.

options.label: Draw Him Out: A Lamp in the Window and Wiggins's Boys on the Roofs.
options.detail: A tiger will come to a tethered goat. You would prefer not to be the goat.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: We'll have the whole street covered, Mr Holmes. If he as much as shows his boots on a chimney-pot, we'll have him by the ankle.

success.outcome: At ten past ten the window across the street gives up a tall shape in a long coat, and a boy on the neighbouring slates shouts. For one moment you see his face: lean, tanned, with a heavy moustache and a hard blue eye. He is gone in the dark by the time the boys reach the roof. But you know him now, and every cabman in London will know him by Friday.

failure.outcome: The lamp is shot out in the first minute, and the boys, who were not told to expect an air-gun, scatter. The Colonel's second shot takes a slate off the roof above your head. By the time you are down the stairs he has gone, and you find that you are shaking, not with fear but with a rage you cannot place.

options.label: Change Your Lodgings Every Night and Trust No Window.
options.detail: A moving target is a harder one. It is also a very tiring life.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: You'll be sleeping in a lodging-house, sir? With the sheets not aired? I never heard the like. I shall pack a bottle.

options.outcome: Four nights in four different houses, in four different coats. You sleep in Whitechapel, in Pimlico, in a cheap hotel in Euston, and once on Watson's sofa. By Thursday you know the fog like a friend, and you have not once been in the same place that Moran thinks you are.

options.label: Send Mrs Hudson to Her Sister in Brighton.
options.detail: She will complain. She will also be a hundred miles from the nearest air-gun.

quote.speaker: Mrs Hudson
quote.text: I'm not frightened, sir, and I'll thank you not to say I am. But I'll go. I never could abide a fuss on a Sunday.

options.outcome: She is gone by the nine o'clock train with a hamper and a hat-box, and a look of faint disapproval. The house is very quiet without her. You note, with a certain surprise, how often you have relied on the sound of her feet in the hall.

echoes.text: You know which lamp-post the Professor's carriage stops beside, and tonight that knowledge is no comfort at all.

S4.title: The Boy Who Did Not Come Back
S4.description: Tuesday 28 April. The boys report at six every evening, in the area, in the order of their seniority, and Wiggins ticks each name on a slate. Tonight the slate has a space in it. Alf, the nippiest, the one who is never caught, has not come home. His mother, a laundress in Seven Dials, has not seen him since Sunday. Wiggins does not say a word. He stands very straight in the kitchen, with his cap in his hands, and his lip is working. It is the first time you have seen him look like what he is, which is fourteen.

options.label: Drop the Work and Find the Boy.
options.detail: A day lost, and more besides. It is not strategy. It is the right thing to do.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: Thank you, Mr Holmes. I never thought you would. I thought you'd say it was one boy and a long war.

options.outcome: You find him on the Wednesday, in a locked cellar off the Highway, with a cut head and a broken wrist, alive and furious. He has told them nothing. He asks, in a thin voice, whether it is still Tuesday, and whether he missed his tea. Wiggins weeps openly. You find it hard to look at either of them.

options.label: Send for Watson to Look Him Over, and Keep Going.
options.detail: Find the boy with Watson's help, and let a doctor do what you cannot.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Show me the child, Holmes, and then get out of the room. I can set a wrist, and you cannot, and you will make a very poor assistant.

options.outcome: Watson finds Alf in an hour, with the help of a laundress and a constable he has known since the war. The wrist is set, the head is bandaged, and the boy is asleep before the doctor has finished his lecture. Watson looks at you across the cot. 'He is somebody's son, Holmes,' he says quietly. 'Remember it.'

options.label: The Boys Knew the Risk. Press the Advantage.
options.detail: One may be lost, and ten be saved. It is a hard sum, and you have done it before.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: Right you are, Mr Holmes. It's what you pay us for. I never did mind the work, sir. I only minded the not knowing.

options.outcome: You turn back to the map. Wiggins stands a minute longer than he need, and then he goes down the area steps without a word. You hear, later, that Alf's body was taken from the river at Limehouse on Thursday. You have the information you wanted. You do not tell anyone what it cost.

echoes.text: It was you who sent him. You can think of nothing else, as you look at the empty space on the slate, and the name written above it.

S5.title: Lestrade's Warning
S5.description: Wednesday 29 April. Lestrade comes up the stairs at an unnatural speed and shuts the door behind him with unnatural care. He has been summoned to the Assistant Commissioner. Questions have been asked about a counting-house in Shoreditch that was entered at night with no warrant, a cab-yard where eleven horses were let loose in the road, and a gentleman in a false beard who was seen in Wapping. 'It isn't the law, Mr Holmes,' he says unhappily. 'It's the other thing. It's a private army, and the Yard won't stand it.' He does not ask whether it is true.

options.label: Promise to Keep Within the Law From This Day.
options.detail: A hard bargain, and a binding one. You are giving up the most useful weapon you had.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: That's all I wanted to hear, Mr Holmes. I'll tell the Chief you've given me your word, and I'll tell him it's the word of a gentleman. Don't make me a liar.

options.outcome: He shakes your hand and holds it for a moment longer than is usual. You tell him that you shall keep it. You mean it. You sit afterwards in the empty room, and consider all that you will be unable to do.

options.label: Hand Him Your Best Lead as a Peace-Offering.
options.detail: Give the Yard something to do. A policeman with a case is a policeman who looks the other way.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: You mean to give me the Shoreditch house? Done. I'll have a dozen men at the door by morning, and nobody will ask how we found it.

options.outcome: He is delighted, and does not hide it. By evening the Yard has a raid of its own, and a headline, and the Chief is smiling. You have lost a thread, but you have bought a season of peace. It is not the worst bargain you have struck.

options.label: Ignore the Warning and Move to New Lodgings.
options.detail: If the Yard cannot protect you, it cannot restrain you. Let it say what it likes.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Then I've told you, Mr Holmes, and I'll have told the Chief. And when it goes wrong, I'll not be the one who has to go and see his friends.

options.outcome: He leaves in a silence that has not a shred of anger in it. That is the worst thing about it. You find a room in Lisson Grove under another name, with a landlady who does not know you, and you lay your papers out in the lamplight. You are alone, and you are working, and you are free.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of a man who has been looked after.

options.label: Let Lestrade Vouch for You.
options.detail: A word from a man the Yard respects. He can do it once. It will mend a good deal, and it will use up what he had.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll say it to the Chief myself, Mr Holmes. I'll say I've known you eleven years. It'll cost me something. I'd as soon you didn't ask what.

options.outcome: Lestrade is gone an hour, and comes back with his collar undone and his hat in his hand. The Chief has agreed, he says, to take another look. The word goes round the building by noon. Doors that were closed are, for the moment, unlocked.

echoes.text: There is a cold list in his hand: the dates, the places, the damage. It has been drawn up with scrupulous fairness, which is much worse than if it had been written in anger.
Lestrade has a note about a tall Englishman with a brown face who has been asking for you at three different cab-ranks. He thinks it is a client.

S6.title: The Banker's Ruin
S6.description: Friday 1 May. The Professor's army fights on gold, and gold is a soft target. All the money, you have learned, runs through a single private bank in Lombard Street, the same in which poor Larch once worked, and the partners of that bank are not conspirators but cowards. They take what they are given. A rumour in the right ear could empty its vaults in three days. A word to the honest directors could close the Professor's accounts overnight. And a letter in the Professor's own hand, correctly forged, could set his two best lieutenants at each other's throats.

options.label: Let Slip a Rumour Through Three City Clerks.
options.detail: A whisper starts a run. A run is a stampede. The Professor's money will be in the street before he has heard the news.

quote.speaker: A City clerk
quote.text: A bank's no stronger than what people think of it, sir. And I've never once known them think well of a bank on a Friday afternoon.

success.outcome: By Monday the pavement in Lombard Street is thick with depositors, and the partners are shouting at each other behind the grille. A third of the Professor's liquid money has been withdrawn, a quarter frozen, and the rest is on the wrong side of the Channel. His lieutenants, who are paid by the week, begin to ask who is going to pay them.

failure.outcome: The rumour is traced to its source within a day, and the partners go straight to the Yard. A police inspector calls, politely, at your lodgings. You have caused a minor panic, injured an honest firm, and failed to injure the dishonest one. The Professor is, if anything, amused.

options.label: Take the Grey Ledger to the Bank's Honest Directors.
options.detail: Show the partners what they have been signing. They can close the accounts lawfully, and in a day.

quote.speaker: The senior partner
quote.text: God help us, Mr Holmes. I have been signing his drafts for nine years. I thought he was a mathematician.

options.outcome: The partners read the ledger for three hours in a silence broken only by groans. By the evening the accounts are frozen, the Professor's name has been struck from the books, and a quiet inspector from the Bank of England is on his way. The law has done your work for you, and has done it better.

options.label: Forge a Letter in the Professor's Hand and Set His Lieutenants at Each Other.
