options.detail: The Professor's own handwriting, in the Professor's own cipher, saying the wrong thing to the wrong man.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: I seen the printer do it, Mr Holmes. He says it's no harder than copying a wall. You only have to see the thing as the man sees it.

success.outcome: The letter goes out by the afternoon post to two of the Professor's most trusted men. By the evening one is dead in a Wapping alley, and the other is on a boat to Antwerp with the contents of the Shoreditch safe. The Professor's organisation, which has stood for ten years, develops a crack you can put a finger in.

failure.outcome: The Professor has a note-paper watermark you did not know about. One of the lieutenants spots the forgery in half a minute, and takes the letter to the Professor himself. The reply, delivered to Baker Street within the hour, is three words long, perfectly legible, and signed with a cross.

echoes.text: You gave Lestrade your word to keep within the law. Each of these three schemes sits very uneasily beside it.

S7.title: Fire in Baker Street
S7.description: Saturday 2 May, a little after two in the morning. You wake to a smell, and then a noise, and then the sight of a long orange tongue licking up the wall of the front staircase. Someone has set fire to 221B Baker Street, and has done it well: paraffin on the stairs, a candle in the cellar, and the door to the street locked from outside. The flames are eating through the floor of the sitting-room, where your papers, your violin, your chemical table and fifteen years of cuttings lie within arm's reach. The Professor has answered you at last.

options.label: Save the Papers: The Ledger, the Index and the Case-Books.
options.detail: Fifteen years of work. Without them the case is a rumour, and the Professor knows it.

quote.speaker: A fireman
quote.text: Get out of there, sir! It's coming through the floor! Sir, for God's sake, leave it!

options.outcome: You go back up the stairs through smoke that tastes of tar, and you come out with two armfuls of paper and the lining of your coat alight. The engine arrives a minute afterwards. By dawn the street is a river of black water, and you are sitting on the kerb in the cold, singed, hoarse and holding a bundle of cuttings like a child.

options.label: Get Everyone Out First: The House Before the Papers.
options.detail: A fire is a fire, whoever started it. Papers can be written again. People cannot.

quote.speaker: The old gentleman from the basement
quote.text: I have lived in this house for twenty years, Mr Holmes, and I never thought to see it go. But I would not have you go back in there for a bundle of old newspaper. Not for the world.

options.outcome: You bring everyone out by the back stair: the lodger on the second floor, the cook, the old gentleman from the basement, and anyone else you can find in the smoke. When the roof falls in, an hour afterwards, you are standing in the road with all of them safe, and none of your papers. You have never felt so poor, or so clear.

options.label: Stand in the Street and Watch the Crowd for the Man Who Lit It.
options.detail: He will not leave. A man who sets a fire must see it burn.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: I've got boys on all four corners, Mr Holmes. If he's here, he's looking at the roof. And a man looking at the roof is easy to see.

success.outcome: He is a short man in a brown coat at the back of the crowd, and he is looking at the roof, and at the end of the street, and at his watch. Wiggins's boys follow him across Marylebone and into Camden Town, to a house with a green door. In the morning you stand outside it with Lestrade's second-best constable. You have found the Professor's lair.

failure.outcome: He is not there. He never was. You stand in the road in your nightshirt, with the roof coming down behind you, and watch a hundred faces lit orange by the fire. Not one of them is his. When you turn back, the staircase has gone, and so has everything you did not carry.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of a man who has been looked after.

echoes.text: The house is empty but for you. Mrs Hudson is a hundred miles away at her sister's in Brighton, and it is the best thing you did all week.
A hundred cabmen now know the Colonel's face. Not one has found him.

S3B.title: The Colonel's Club
S3B.description: Tuesday 28 April, morning. The Colonel belongs to a club in a quiet street off Pall Mall, a high, dim, comfortable place of leather chairs and old Army men and a smell of cold roast beef, where nobody has ever been known to ask a question. It is his one weakness: he comes at three every afternoon for a rubber of whist and a glass of port. If you can learn his hours, his habits and the way he leaves, you can be waiting for him, rather than the other way about. It is the only time in the day that the finest shot in the Indian Army is not carrying a gun.

options.label: Take a Waiter's Place for One Afternoon.
options.detail: A white jacket and a tray. A waiter is the most invisible creature in London, and the one who hears the most.

quote.speaker: The club steward
quote.text: You'll do, I suppose, if you keep your eyes down and your mouth shut. A man's a waiter for the evening. He'll not be a gentleman till he's left the building.

success.outcome: For five hours you carry port and cigars through the card-room, with your eyes on the carpet. The Colonel does not look at you once. You learn his table, his chair, his stick, the hour he calls for his cab and the door he leaves by, and the odd, soft, careful way he carries his walking-stick, which never touches the ground.

failure.outcome: A hard blue eye rests on your hands as you pour. He says nothing, and he does not look again. But at five o'clock the steward, with great apology, informs you that your services are no longer required. You leave by the area steps. The Colonel's cab is already at the kerb, and he is already in it.

options.label: Bribe the Hall Porter for the Colonel's Habits.
options.detail: A porter sees everyone, and is paid by nobody to remember. A sovereign changes that.

quote.speaker: The hall porter
quote.text: Three o'clock, sir, every day but Sunday. A rubber and a glass of port, and out by the Pall Mall door at six. He always has his stick. Funny thing, he never leans on it.

options.outcome: The porter is a long, dry, cautious man who has sold nothing in thirty years, and he sells you the Colonel's day for five pounds, at a price he does not discuss. You come away with an hour-by-hour account and the faint taste of something not quite clean.

options.label: Ask Watson, Who Served in the Army, for Old Friends.
options.detail: A man who was in Afghanistan knows men who were in India. There is a whole society of them, and every one has a story about the Colonel.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I know three men who served under him, Holmes. They never spoke well of him, and they never spoke ill. It is a curious thing. They only ever lowered their voices.

options.outcome: Watson writes four letters before supper and receives two answers by breakfast. Between them they give you the Colonel's character, his hours, his opinion of the Government, and a story of a tiger that is told of him in three regiments. It is the most useful dinner of the month.
options.requiresHint: Needs Watson's trust

S5B.title: The Printer Turns
S5B.description: Thursday 30 April. The Clerkenwell printer, a lean, tidy, ink-fingered man named Quill, has not slept for three nights, and it shows in the way he holds a cup. He sent for you through a boy with a bundle of proofs and a note in a very beautiful hand. He has spent twenty years setting type for the Professor's friends, he says, and has never once asked what the letters said. But there is a limit, and he has reached it, and he would like very much to be told what to do.

options.label: Offer Him Protection and a New Name, in Exchange for the Plates.
options.detail: He wants out. You can give it to him. It will cost a little, and it will make you responsible.

quote.speaker: Mr Quill
quote.text: I should like to emigrate, sir. To Canada, I think. They have newspapers there, I'm told, and very few cheques. I'll give you the plates if you'll give me a berth.

options.outcome: You put him on a ship at Tilbury a fortnight later, under another name, with his tools in a wooden box. He weeps at the rail. The plates are in your coat, and every one of them is a lie that would have ruined an honest man, and you will not use any of them but one. It is the best bargain of the war.

options.label: Tell Him He Will Hang Unless He Gives You Everything.
options.detail: He is a frightened man. A frightened man will give you what he is told to. It is a cheap way to win, and an ugly one.

quote.speaker: Mr Quill
quote.text: You'll hang me, Mr Holmes? I did not think a gentleman would say a thing like that. I thought I'd come to a friend.

options.outcome: He gives you everything: the plates, the type, the proofs and the names. He gives them with his hands shaking and his eyes on the floor. When he has gone you find that you do not want to look at them. It is a victory, and a perfectly good one. It is not the kind of victory that you would choose to describe to Watson.

options.label: Thank Him and Tell Him to Go Home.
options.detail: You cannot protect him. You cannot spend what you have not got. Send him back to the work he knows.

quote.speaker: Mr Quill
quote.text: Go home, sir? But they will know that I came. They always know. I do not think that I shall see Christmas, if I go home.

options.outcome: He stands for a moment in the doorway, small and grey and extremely tidy, as if waiting for you to change your mind. You do not. He puts on his hat, with great care, and goes. You hear, a week later, that the shop is shut and the shutters are up. Nobody knows where he has gone.

echoes.text: You remember a young woman on your sofa in February, and a plain neat type with a flaw in the lower-case 'g'. It is his hand. He wrote those letters to Miss Crewe, and did not know why.
You remember the courier on the Heath, and the bundle of printed letters under his arm. They were set in this room.

S6B.title: Wiggins's Quarrel
S6B.description: Friday 1 May, evening. The boys have gathered in the kitchen at Baker Street, as they do, but tonight there is no ginger-beer and no ham. They stand in a shuffling half-circle with their caps in their hands, looking at Wiggins, and Wiggins is looking at his boots. He has been chosen to say it. The boys are tired, he says, and hungry, and some of them have not been home in a week. They do not mind the work. They mind not being told how it ends. They would like, if it is not too much trouble, to be told whom they are fighting, and why.

options.label: Stand Before Them and Tell Them Everything, and Take the Blame.
options.detail: You owe them the truth. It will not be pleasant, and they will think the less of you for the honesty.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: Well, that's all right then, Mr Holmes. I told 'em you'd say. I told 'em you weren't the sort to leave a lad without an answer. It's only that nobody ever did before.

options.outcome: You tell them about the Professor, and the ledger, and the clerk, and the brick on the roof. They listen with an attention you have never had from a jury. When you have finished a very small boy at the back says, in a voice that carries, that he thought it was something like that, and the room breaks into a roar of laughter. You have not been so glad of a laugh in months.

options.label: Pay Them Double and Promise It Ends on Monday.
options.detail: A fair wage and a kind lie. It will keep them with you, and it may cost you the right to say you did not promise.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: A week of double, Mr Holmes? Gor. I'll tell 'em. And I'll tell 'em it's Monday, and not before. If it turns out not to be Monday, that'll be on you, and I'll not say a word.

options.outcome: The money is counted out on the kitchen table in sixpences, and the boys look at it as though it were a mountain. They go home that night with something in their pockets for the first time in a month. It is a sound arrangement. You know, as you shut the door, that you have promised something you cannot swear to keep.

options.label: Tell Any Who Want to Go Home That They Are Free to Go.
options.detail: Release them from it. Some will stay, and some will not. The ones who stay will be the better for it.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: You mean it, Mr Holmes? Anyone? Well. I'll stay, of course. But I'll say it's a queer thing to be asked.

options.outcome: Seven of the twelve stay. Five go home, with a shilling each, looking very much relieved and slightly ashamed. Wiggins watches them go with his lip set. Afterwards he says, to nobody, that it was the right thing, and that he would not have had the courage. It is a smaller army, and an honester one.

echoes.text: Nobody mentions Alf. Nobody looks at the empty place on the slate. It is as if the room were holding its breath.
Alf is there, with his arm in a sling, sitting on a stool by the range, and he is the only one who is smiling.

S8.title: The Wharf Approach
S8.description: Tuesday 5 May, dusk. A note arrives at the lodging in Lisson Grove, delivered by a boy who has no idea who gave it to him: a time, a place, and a single initial. The place is a disused wharf at Limehouse, a quarter-mile of black timber and tarry water, with a derelict warehouse at the end. The Professor will be there alone. Or he will not. Everything you have done since January has tended to this: the clerk, the ledger, the boys, the fire, the money. You have an hour before the tide, and a choice of how to come.

options.label: By Water, in a Lighterman's Boat With Wiggins's Boys.
options.detail: The river is the one road that nobody watches, because everybody forgets that it is there.

quote.speaker: A lighterman
quote.text: I've taken a good many gentlemen to a good many wharves, sir. I never yet took one who wanted to be there. Sit in the middle and keep your hands inboard.

options.outcome: The boat slides out of the dark under Wapping Stairs with its oars muffled in sacking. The tide is on the turn, and the wharf comes up on the left like a long black tooth. There is no light in the warehouse. There is, on the water-stairs, a single figure, very tall, with a lantern shaded in his hand.

options.label: Over the Warehouse Roof on a Rope.
options.detail: A harder way in, and a quieter one. You will come down on the Professor from above, which is not a direction he has considered.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: It's twenty-two foot, Mr Holmes, and the slates are loose on the north side. I'd not ask a lad to do it. But I've seen you do worse in the rain.

success.outcome: The rope goes round a chimney and you go down it hand over hand, with the black river under you and the old warehouse a great sloping shadow. The skylight gives to your knife. You drop into a loft that smells of tar and rats and dust, and from the dark below you hear, quite distinctly, a man humming a tune.

failure.outcome: A slate gives under your boot, and you go down fifteen feet in a clatter of tiles, and come up against a beam with a crack that you feel in your teeth. Below, a lantern goes out. A door slams, and then another. You are, quite plainly, expected.

options.label: Walk Down the Quay in the Open, With a Lantern.
options.detail: A bold, plain and perfectly honest way to arrive. It tells the Professor that you are not afraid of him.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You have come by the front, Mr Holmes. I confess I had not thought of that. It is a tactic of great simplicity, and I find it rather moving.

options.outcome: You walk the whole quarter-mile in full view, in your own coat, with a lantern swinging from your hand. Nobody shoots. The warehouse door is open, and the lamps inside are lit, and the Professor, from the end of the passage, lifts his hat to you as though you had come to dinner.

echoes.text: The seven who stayed are the best of them, and every one of them knows it. They are very quiet.
You know the house with the green door in Camden Town, and the Professor knows that you know it. It is the only reason he has agreed to this meeting.

S8B.title: Inside the Warehouse
S8B.description: Tuesday night. The warehouse is a long, black, echoing barn, with a gantry running the length of the wall and a smell of tar, tallow and wet iron. At the far end a door stands open on a lamplit office, and from the gantry above it comes a very small sound: the click of a brass catch on a long, oddly-shaped stick. Colonel Moran has been on that gantry since noon, and he has the whole floor in his sights. The Professor, in the office, is waiting. Nothing will happen to him until the Colonel is dealt with, and the Colonel is not a man who deals.

options.label: Take the Colonel First.
options.detail: He is a very fine shot and a very poor loser. If you know his habits, you know where he will stand.

quote.speaker: Colonel Moran
quote.text: I had hoped, Mr Holmes, that you would come. It is such a very long time since I had the chance of anything worth a bullet.

options.requiresHint: Needs to know the Colonel's face or his habits

success.outcome: You know where he stands, because you have watched him stand there for a week in a different place. You are under the gantry before he has finished raising the stick, and the iron stair rings once under your boot. He fires, and the bolt goes wide into a barrel of tar. The fight is brief and extremely ugly, and when it is over the Colonel is on his back, with his arm in a sling of his own braces and an expression of mild affront.

failure.outcome: He is a better judge of your habits than you are of his. The air-gun coughs once from the dark, and something takes you through the left shoulder like a hot iron. You go down behind a crate with a hiss of breath. He does not fire again. He is not a man to waste a bullet on a man who is already fallen, and he does not trouble to hurry.

options.label: Send the Boys Round the Back to Cut the Lamp-Oil.
options.detail: A man who shoots in the dark needs light. Take away the light, and take the gantry away with it.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: We'll do it, Mr Holmes. Three boys to the back and four to the roof. We've been cutting lamps off since we could walk. You'll hear when it goes.

options.outcome: The warehouse goes dark in the space of three heartbeats, and a roar goes up from the gantry that has more of astonishment than rage. By the time the Colonel has found a match, there are seven small figures on the gantry with a rope, and a very large and very surprised soldier is going down the stair with his hands tied. Wiggins looks at you from the shadow and grins.

options.label: Send the Colonel a Forged Note From the Professor.
options.detail: The printer's hand, a plausible message and a boy at the door. A man who has been told to go may go.

quote.speaker: Mr Quill
quote.text: It will be perfect, sir. It will be better than perfect. It will look as if the Professor had written it on a Sunday, which is when his hand is always at its worst.

options.outcome: The note is delivered by a boy in a green apron, with a perfect indifference. The Colonel reads it twice by the light of a match, in the dark, and says one soft word, and goes down the stair with his stick under his arm. He is on the pavement before he realises that the Professor never wrote it, and by then the warehouse has a policeman at every door.

options.label: Go Straight for the Professor and Ignore the Gantry.
options.detail: A foolish, brave and perfectly open way to proceed. He may not shoot. He may.

quote.speaker: Colonel Moran
quote.text: Oh, I shall shoot, Mr Holmes. I merely wish to see how far you intend to walk first.

options.outcome: You go down the long floor at a walk, with your hands in your pockets and your eyes on the lamplit door, and the whole of your back an open invitation. A bolt buries itself in the planks a foot to your left, and then another a foot to the right. He is placing them, you realise, like a man sketching a frame about a picture. At the door you stop, and turn, and bow. You do not hear what he says.

options.label: Let Wiggins Lead the Boys In.
options.detail: They will do what he says, and he will do what you say. It is a chain of trust that has never before been tried in a warehouse.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: Leave it to me, Mr Holmes. We've done it before, in a cellar in Bermondsey, and nobody got hurt but a pig. I'll have the Colonel's gun off him before he's had time to be surprised.

options.outcome: Wiggins goes up the wall like a cat, and the boys go after him in a stream. There is a short, silent, comic struggle on the gantry, a fall of tarpaulin, and a very large man sitting on a very small boy. The air-gun is passed down the line like a bucket at a fire.
options.requiresHint: Needs Wiggins's full trust

echoes.text: The lighterman's boat is tied below the water-stairs, with its oars shipped and its lantern covered. It is a quiet way out.
You hang from a joist in the roof, with the rope round your wrist and the whole of the floor beneath you.
You came by the front, with a lantern. Everyone in the building knows it.

S8C.title: The Professor at Bay
S8C.description: Tuesday night, in the lamplit office at the end of the warehouse. The Professor sits behind a deal table with his hands folded and his head swaying slowly from side to side, and he looks, in the thin light, rather like an old and extremely intelligent snake in a drawing-room. He does not offer to rise. He has lost, he says in a pleasant voice, a good deal of money in the last fortnight, and a rather greater quantity of his patience. He wishes to know on what terms the matter may be concluded. Everything you have done since January has tended to this. If you are going to end it, it is going to end here, one way or another.

options.label: Close the Net: Everything You Have, and Not a Gap in It.
options.detail: The Colonel down, the money gone, the lieutenants at each other's throats. He has nothing left to bargain with.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: I have made a mistake, Mr Holmes, and it is a small mistake, and I made it three months ago. It was to suppose that you would be sensible.

options.outcome: You do not need the pistol in your pocket. You lay it all out for him in a level voice: the bank, the ledger, the lieutenant who is dead and the lieutenant who is on a boat. His face does not change, but his head stops swaying. He says one word, which is your name. And then the river takes him, or he takes the river; you are never quite sure which.
options.requiresHint: Needs the Colonel beaten and the Professor's money or men broken

options.label: Break Him Anyway: Throw Everything You Have at the Table.
options.detail: The ledger, the money, the rivalry, the fire. You have laid your wires. If you are short a wire, you will find out now.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You are bluffing, Mr Holmes. It is a charming thing to see in a man of your attainments. I shall ask you, with great courtesy, to show me the hand.

success.outcome: You do not need the pistol in your pocket. The Professor stands at the end of the wharf in the thin light, and you lay it all out for him: the bank, the ledger, the dead lieutenant, the printer's proofs. His face does not change, but his head stops swaying. He says one word, which is your name. And then the river takes him, or he takes the river; you are never quite sure which.

failure.outcome: He has brought more men than you were told, and fewer scruples than you hoped. They come out of the warehouse in a line, and you go over the wharf-edge into the black water with a boy's cry in your ears. You are pulled out at Wapping Stairs by a lighterman, half-drowned, to find that Baker Street has been quietly sold to a stranger.

options.label: Take the Professor's Terms.
options.detail: A peace on his conditions. He keeps London, and you keep your life, your name, and a very large sum of money.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: I knew you were an intelligent man, Mr Holmes. The pity of it is that intelligence is so seldom accompanied by anything else.

options.outcome: He nods, very slightly, as a man nods who has been proved right. The paper is in a clerk's hand and it is a masterpiece of discretion. You sign. It is quiet on the wharf, and the tide is turning, and you do not look back at the fire-blackened window across the river.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs you to have listened to his offer

options.label: Turn Round and Walk Away.
options.detail: You have done enough. You have lost enough. Let him have the river.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I have always thought there was a time to put down the glass and go home to bed. I think you had better find it, Holmes, before you find a worse one.

options.outcome: You turn your back on the wharf and walk the length of Narrow Street in the first grey of morning. No one calls after you. The tide runs out under the piers, and the fog comes up behind you like a curtain being drawn.

echoes.text: The Professor's money is frozen, and his men have not been paid in nine days. This is a desperate man, however calmly he sits.
One lieutenant is dead and the other is on a boat. The Professor's organisation has a crack in it, and he knows who put it there.
The Colonel is trussed in the corner of the warehouse, silent and humiliated, with an expression of profound disapproval.

C1.title: Victoria Station
C1.description: Saturday 25 April, a quarter to ten. The Continental express stands at the platform with steam rising from beneath it like breath from a horse, and the barrier is thick with porters, trunks and a smell of coal and wet umbrellas. Somewhere in the crowd, you are sure, there is a man whose business it is to see who goes aboard. You are the most easily recognised man in London, and you have one hour to cease to be so. Watson stands at your elbow with his bag in his hand and no idea what you intend, which is exactly how you want him.

options.label: Go as an Aged Italian Priest.
options.detail: A black soutane, a stoop, a broad hat, and a vague, courteous bewilderment. Nobody looks twice at a priest.

quote.speaker: A porter
quote.text: Beg pardon, Father? You'd be wanting the boat-train, I dare say. It's the second on your left, and I'll see your boxes are put aboard.

success.outcome: You shuffle down the platform with a breviary and a basket, and ask a porter, in a thick and plausible English, to have your baggage sent on to Paris. A tall man by the bookstall watches the whole performance and sees an old priest. Watson, who has not been told, passes you twice before his eyes widen. He has the grace to say nothing at all.

failure.outcome: A porter drops a trunk, and you step round it with a too-quick, too-young stride. A man at the barrier looks at your feet and then at your face. By the time the guard has blown his whistle, a boy with a telegraph form is running down the platform in the other direction.

options.label: Travel Openly, First Class, in Your Own Name.
options.detail: A sealed compartment with the blinds drawn. If he wants to know where you are, let him know. It will be hard for him to act.

quote.speaker: The guard
quote.text: First-class, sir, and the blinds down. I'll see that nobody disturbs you. There's a gentleman asking questions at the bookstall, but he'll get no answers from me.

options.outcome: The sealed compartment is warm and quiet and as safe as a vault. It is also, you cannot help remembering, a vault with a single door. By Tonbridge Watson has fallen asleep with his bag on his knee, and you sit upright, with a pistol in your coat, watching the green fields go past.

options.label: Send Watson Ahead With the Luggage and Follow on the Later Train.
options.detail: Two travellers are a trail. One is a gentleman on his own errand. Split the party and join it again at the sea.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I do not like to leave you, Holmes. But I shall go. I shall also be extremely cross if I find you have been run down by a hansom.

options.outcome: Watson goes aboard alone, indignant and bewildered, and you watch him out of sight. For the first time since January, you have no one at your elbow. The platform seems very large. You take the next train, with a newspaper held high, and are all the way to Canterbury before you realise how much you have missed his voice.

options.label: Pawn Your Watch for the Fare.
options.detail: A gold half-hunter, a gift from a grateful client. It will buy the tickets and leave you with a little in hand.

quote.speaker: A pawnbroker near Victoria
quote.text: Fifteen shillings in the pound, sir, and a card with your name on it. They always come back. I have never in my life been surprised to see a gentleman again.

options.outcome: You cross to a small shop in the arcade, and the old man behind the counter puts a glass in his eye and looks at the watch for a long time. 'Six pounds,' he says. 'It is a very good watch.' You say that it is. You take the money, and go to the train, and feel, for the first time since January, quite perfectly poor.

options.label: Take the Route You Planned in February.
options.detail: Written in your own cipher on the inside of a cigarette-case, and booked, and paid. It is the one thing in this whole business that has gone to plan.

quote.speaker: The travel agent
quote.text: Ah, Mr Dubois. Your tickets are in order, sir, and your places in the second carriage from the end. I am told the boat will be on time. I never say so, but I am told.

options.outcome: You go straight to your carriage, past a crowd and a smell of coal and wet umbrellas, with the ticket in your hand and not a flutter in your pulse. It is the plainest, quietest, most boring departure in the history of the Continental express, and you enjoy it exceedingly.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs a route planned in February

C2.title: The Special at Canterbury
C2.description: Saturday, a little before noon. The train has stopped at Canterbury to take on water, and in the pause a long, low whistle sounds up the line. A special locomotive, with a single carriage coupled to it, thunders into the station at a speed that blows the porters' caps off, and goes through without slackening. For one half-second a face is visible at the carriage window: long, domed, white, swaying from side to side. The Professor has chartered a train to catch you, and has missed you by three minutes. He will not miss you twice.

options.label: Leave the Train at Canterbury and Let the Special Pass.
options.detail: He is ahead of you, now. A man who is ahead of you has to turn round.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are quite sure of this, Holmes? I confess I feel a most unheroic wish to be in Dover by dark.

options.outcome: You step down onto the platform with your bags and watch the train that was supposed to carry you steam away to the coast. An hour later the special comes back through the station in the opposite direction, empty of passengers but one. The Professor does not look out of his window. He is too angry, you think, to look at anything at all.

options.label: Stay Aboard. It Is a Bluff to Make You Run.
options.detail: A man who chases with a special train is a man who cannot know where you are. Keep your seat.

quote.speaker: The guard
quote.text: We'll be at Dover in the hour, sir, and not a minute behind. I'd not trouble yourself about trains that go by.

success.outcome: You are right. The special had no plan for Dover except to be there, and by the time it has been turned it has lost the best part of an afternoon. You walk the Dover quay in the dusk with a telegram in your pocket and Watson at your side, and for once you have gained a day.

failure.outcome: You are wrong. A stranger in a grey coat boards at Ashford and moves up the corridor to the next compartment, and does not go away. At Dover you are followed down the pier, at a distance of twenty yards, by a man who is not even trying to hide. It is a long, cold crossing.

options.label: Telegraph Mycroft From the Platform.
options.detail: A single line in the cipher your family used as boys. He will know what to do before you do.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: A credit has been opened for you at the Crédit Lyonnais in Brussels. Do not thank me. Merely try to stay alive until it is spent.

options.outcome: The reply comes in twelve minutes, which is the speed of a man who has been expecting you. A letter of credit awaits at Brussels, and two foreign officials in Calais have been made to remember that they owe the Foreign Office a favour. You put the paper in your pocket-book. For once you are not alone.

echoes.text: You are still in the priest's clothes. Watson, to your lasting admiration, has not once laughed at them.
A tall man with a violin-case is standing at the far end of the platform, looking at the clock. You do not look twice. You do not need to.

C3.title: The Night Crossing
C3.description: Sunday 26 April, aboard the night steamer from Dover to Calais. The sea is black and heavy, and the little boat rolls like a drunk. The saloon is half empty, and a handful of passengers are asleep in their coats. Watson has said very little since Canterbury. He sits across from you on the horsehair bench with his collar up, regarding you with the expression of a man who has been asked to jump off a cliff and told, afterwards, that it was for his own good. 'Holmes,' he says at last. 'I think I had better know what this is about.'

options.label: Tell Him the Whole of It, From January.
options.detail: He has earned it. He has also been in danger since Canterbury without knowing why.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Moriarty. Good God. I have read his book on the asteroid, you know. I thought it a very dull sort of work. I find I must revise my opinion of the man.

options.outcome: It takes the whole of the crossing. You tell him the clerk, the ledger, the brick, the dray, the visit, the Monday. When you come to the end the lights of Calais are coming up out of the dark, and Watson has taken out his notebook, put it away again, and given you his hand. 'I am with you,' he says. 'Don't suppose I am doing it for the sake of the notes.'

options.label: Tell Him Only That You Are Hunted.
options.detail: The truth in a small bottle. It is enough to explain the flight, and not enough to worry him further.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I see. A man of some importance, with a long arm and a short temper. I do not suppose you will tell me his name. Well. I have never needed it to be on your side.

options.outcome: He accepts it with a nod, and asks nothing more. He sleeps, in the end, on the bench, with his head against the panelling and his bag clutched to his chest. You do not. You watch the black windows and the Calais lights, and think that a friend's trust is an odd sort of burden: lighter than a lie, and heavier than the truth.

options.label: Tell Him Nothing. The Fewer Who Know, the Fewer He Can Hurt.
options.detail: A kindness, perhaps. Or the loneliest kind of cowardice.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Very well, Holmes. I shall not ask again. But I should like you to know that I find it a good deal harder to be trusted with nothing than with anything.

options.outcome: You tell him that it is a matter you cannot discuss. He looks at you for a long while, and then takes out a small paper-covered book and reads it with a studied concentration. You watch him turn four pages without moving his eyes. The sea gets up outside, and the saloon lamp swings, and neither of you speaks again until Calais.

options.label: Lie By for a Day and Do Nothing Whatever.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Not a word about the Professor until tomorrow. I have asked the landlord for a fire and a bottle of something Swiss, and I shall sit up, and you shall sleep.

options.outcome: You sleep for fourteen hours in a feather bed in a room that smells of wood-smoke, and wake to rain on the shutters and the sound of Watson turning the pages of a very old Baedeker. For the first time in a week you are hungry.

C4.title: The Telegram at Brussels
C4.description: Monday 27 April. The Hôtel de la Poste in Brussels has a view of a wet square and a bronze general, and a concierge who has seen a great many Englishmen who did not wish to be found. At five o'clock a telegram comes for 'Mr Henri Dubois', which is no name of yours, and you open it with the feeling of a man putting his hand into a bag in the dark. It is from London. It tells you how the raids went. It does not tell you whether the man you are running from was among those taken.

options.label: Wire Lestrade Everything You Know of Moran's Likely Road.
options.detail: Your knowledge of the Colonel's habits is the Yard's best chance of finding him. It is also a signed letter to anyone who reads your telegrams.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: Your wire received. We have the Colonel's club, his landlord and his tailor. He has not been seen since Friday. If he's on the Continent, Mr Holmes, you will see him before we do.

options.outcome: The wire is four hundred words long, and costs two pounds in the hotel's best English. The reply is brisk. Scotland Yard has put a watch on the Channel ports, and sent a detective-sergeant to Brussels. You are not alone, and you did not need telling that you ought to feel safer.

options.label: Say Nothing and Leave by the Early Train.
options.detail: A telegram is a trail. The less you leave, the harder you are to follow.

quote.speaker: The concierge
quote.text: Monsieur will be wanting his bill at five in the morning? Certainly. I shall not remember what monsieur looked like. It is a failing of mine.

options.outcome: You put the telegram in the stove and go to bed in your clothes. In the morning you leave by the first train, with the hotel's bill paid in cash and not a word left behind. Watson says nothing, but his face is the colour of a man who has been woken at four. London goes on without you.

options.label: Wait a Day in Brussels and Read the English Papers.
options.detail: News is power. A day lost may buy you a week's advantage, or give the enemy the one night he needs.

quote.speaker: A newspaper vendor
quote.text: The Times, monsieur, the Standard, the Pall Mall. All from yesterday, you understand. In Brussels everything is a little behind, and one finds it restful.

success.outcome: The English papers are full of Monday's raids: thirty-one arrested, a bishop's secretary in the dock, a retired Colonel of Marines hiding in a wardrobe. The Professor is not named. But in the Standard, in a paragraph at the bottom of a column, you read that a stranger was asked for at the Gare du Nord by name, and left without a bag. He is coming through France.

failure.outcome: The English papers are full of Monday's raids, and tell you nothing that is not already in your pocket. The day is wasted. And that evening, in the hotel bar, a quiet Englishman takes the seat beside yours and orders a lemonade, which you have never seen an Englishman do. You leave by the kitchen door.

echoes.text: The grey ledger is in the false bottom of your case. It is worth more than the whole of your luggage together, and weighs a good deal less than your conscience.
The telegram is warmer than you expected. The Yard has taken a larger bag than you dared hope, and a score of the Professor's chief men are in cells.
The telegram is colder than you expected. The Yard has taken the small men and missed the great ones, and a score of the Professor's people are still at large.

C5.title: A Stranger at Strasbourg
C5.description: Wednesday 29 April. The Hôtel de la Cigogne has a long dining-room, a red-faced landlord, and a clock that strikes everything twice. At the table d'hôte tonight sits an elderly English gentleman with a white moustache and a Panama hat, who has been introduced to you by the landlord with a flourish, and who has asked, in the most casual of voices, whether you are by any chance acquainted with a Professor Moriarty. He wishes to know because he is a fellow mathematician, and he has a small point about the binomial theorem.

options.label: Take the Old Gentleman Aside and Confront Him.
options.detail: He is either an enthusiast or an assassin. A direct question will tell you which, one way or the other.

quote.speaker: The Panama-hatted stranger
quote.text: A small point only, my dear sir. Nothing that needs to concern a man who has no acquaintance with the gentleman. You say you have none?

success.outcome: You take him by the elbow into the garden and quote the first sentence of the treatise, and he finishes it, in a Wapping accent that does not belong to his hat. He goes white. By the time the landlord has found a candle he has taken to his heels, and you hold the Panama, and a card with a name you recognise from the Professor's ledger.

failure.outcome: He is a very gentle old gentleman, in the end, and a very vexed one, and what follows is a most embarrassing quarter of an hour. He is a retired schoolmaster from Tunbridge Wells who has read a great many books on mathematics. The landlord is outraged. Watson, across the room, hides his face in a napkin.

options.label: Slip Away in the Night and Change Trains Twice.
options.detail: If he is an assassin, he will lose the trail. If he is a mathematician, he will be a little hurt.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I have packed the bags, Holmes. I wish I had been told that we were leaving. I had begun to look forward to the cutlets.

options.outcome: You leave by a side door at one in the morning, and change at Kehl and again at Basel, and take a third train in the wrong direction. By the morning you are in a village you cannot find on any map, with a rolled umbrella and a blister on your heel. It is a very tiring way to be safe.

options.label: Feed Him a False Itinerary and Watch Where It Goes.
options.detail: Leave a trail to Marseilles on the table, and see which of the waiters picks it up.

quote.speaker: A waiter
quote.text: The gentleman has left a paper on the table, monsieur. I will take it to the landlord for safe keeping, if monsieur has no objection.

options.outcome: You leave the timetable on the table with Marseilles ringed in red. In the morning the paper is gone. An hour later, on the platform at the station, you see the waiter in conversation with a man in a grey coat. He gives the man the paper. The man gives him a coin. You turn the other way, and board the northbound train.

options.label: Lie By for a Day and Do Nothing Whatever.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Not a word about the Professor until tomorrow. I have asked the landlord for a fire and a bottle of something Swiss, and I shall sit up, and you shall sleep.

options.outcome: You sleep for fourteen hours in a feather bed in a room that smells of wood-smoke, and wake to rain on the shutters and the sound of Watson turning the pages of a very old Baedeker. For the first time in a week you are hungry.

echoes.text: The priest's clothes are in the bottom of your trunk, and you have not worn them since Brussels. You wonder whether to put them on again.

C6.title: The Lake in the Rain
C6.description: Friday 1 May. Geneva is wet. The lake is the colour of pewter, and the mountains are somewhere behind a curtain of grey, and the whole city smells of fish, damp wool and chocolate. You have a room on the third floor of a hotel on the quay, and Watson has the one next door, and for the first time since Victoria no one is following you. It is almost unbearable. Your hands shake on the window-sill. You have not slept for more than three hours at a stretch since the fourth of January, and the strain of it is beginning, at last, to show.

options.label: Rest for Two Days. The Chase Can Wait.
options.detail: A man who cannot hold a pistol steady is no use to anyone. But you will lose a day, and the Professor will gain one.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to stay in your room for forty-eight hours, Holmes, with the blinds drawn and a hot-water bottle, and I shall bring you soup. That is a medical order, and I shall not hear a word against it.

options.outcome: You sleep for fourteen hours, wake to rain, eat Watson's soup, and sleep again. On the third morning you are well enough to read a newspaper without feeling the print swim. It has cost you the freshness of the trail. But you can feel your own mind again, like a hand at the end of an arm.

options.label: Push On Over the Pass to Interlaken Without Delay.
options.detail: A guide, two mules, and the best part of a day's climb. It is the road a hunted man would not choose, and so the best.

quote.speaker: A mountain guide
quote.text: The Gemmi in this weather, monsieur? It is not a path for gentlemen. But for a gentleman who pays in advance, it is a path like any other.

options.outcome: The climb takes eleven hours, in sleet and wind, with the mules complaining at every switchback. At the top you stand in a ring of white mountains, and Watson, panting, says that it is the most remarkable view he has ever seen and he hopes never to see it again. Nobody can have followed you here. Nobody sensible would try.

options.label: Write to Mycroft for Money and a Quiet Hand.
options.detail: A long letter, in the family cipher, with every detail. It is a risk to put it on paper, and a greater risk not to.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Your letter is received. I enclose a draft on a Swiss bank which you will find does not ask questions. The Foreign Office has no idea where you are, and would be distressed to learn that I do.

options.outcome: The answer reaches you in four days, but the first, brief telegram arrives in four hours: 'Letter received. Stay where you are. M.' You do not stay. But the brief message is a little thing, and it warms you more than it ought.

options.label: Lie By for a Day and Do Nothing Whatever.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Not a word about the Professor until tomorrow. I have asked the landlord for a fire and a bottle of something Swiss, and I shall sit up, and you shall sleep.

options.outcome: You sleep for fourteen hours in a feather bed in a room that smells of wood-smoke, and wake to rain on the shutters and the sound of Watson turning the pages of a very old Baedeker. For the first time in a week you are hungry.

echoes.text: The man in the green hat is somewhere behind you on the line. You wonder how much he told, and to whom.
The guide in the hotel hall remarks, as if it were a trifle, that a gentleman with a long coat and a stick has asked for you by name.

C7.title: The Inn at the Foot of the Falls
C7.description: Sunday 3 May. Meiringen is a village of dark wooden houses in a green valley, with a church, a river and a great grey wall of mountain at the end of the street. The proprietor of the English inn is a gentle, broad-faced Swiss named Steiler, who spreads a clean cloth, apologises for the weather, and recommends, as one recommends the sunset, the Reichenbach Falls, a mile and a half up the valley, where the river drops three hundred feet into a black gorge. Watson wants to see them. You have a feeling, standing in the doorway, that you ought not to go.

options.label: Spend the Evening With Watson, Talking of Anything but the Case.
options.detail: Wine, cheese, an old song or two. You do not often waste an evening. It is time you did.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I should like to say that I have enjoyed this journey, Holmes. I know that is not what it has been. But I have not laughed so much since the Sholtos' wine-cellar.

options.outcome: You talk of old cases and old friends, of a rainy night in Dartmoor and a fogbound night in Wapping, and of the sort of things men talk of when they are not afraid. Watson sings, badly, in the dark. You look at him over the rim of the glass and think it a very long way back to the Strand.

options.label: Sit Up With the Case-Book and Set Down the Whole Story.
options.detail: If anything should happen, there should be a record. You write quickly, and with an odd steadiness.

quote.speaker: The proprietor
quote.text: You will need more candles, sir. I will bring some. I have noticed that the English gentlemen who write in the evenings are always short of candles.

options.outcome: You fill thirty pages in a clear small hand. It is every detail you have, every name, every address, every date, in an order that could be followed by a stranger. You put it in an envelope and write on it, after a moment's thought, the name of your brother. The inn is very quiet. A dog barks somewhere down the valley.

options.label: Watch the Road From the Upper Window All Night.
options.detail: A pistol on the sill, the lamp turned down, and a view of the only road that leads to the Falls.

quote.speaker: The proprietor
quote.text: There was a gentleman asked for you this afternoon, sir. A tall gentleman, English, with a very brown face. I said you were not here. He seemed not to believe me.

options.outcome: At two in the morning, by the light of a quarter moon, a tall man in a long coat comes up the road from the valley, very slowly, with an odd-shaped walking-stick under his arm. He stops under the lamp, looks up at your window, and touches his hat. He is perfectly polite. He walks on, towards the Falls, and does not look back.

echoes.text: On the table in the hall of the inn there is a violin-case that does not belong to anyone, and nobody will say whose it is.

C8.title: A Message From the Hotel
C8.description: Monday 4 May, a little after noon. You have been out on the Reichenbach path, and have just come back, when a lad in a green apron comes running down the lane with a note, and an urgent manner. It is addressed to Dr Watson. An English lady, it says in a firm, small, woman's hand, is lying at the hotel at the Falls, dying of the last stage of consumption, and has been told that there is an English doctor in the valley. She asks that he will come at once. The note is on good paper. The hand is very careful. And you have known, from the first line, that it is a lie.

options.label: Tell Watson It Is a Trap, and Keep Him Beside You.
options.detail: He will not like it. He will also not be at the other end of the valley when you most want him.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: A trap. Of course it is. Do you suppose, Holmes, that I have walked eleven hundred miles after you in order to be tricked out of the last mile by a woman in a note?

options.outcome: You hold the note to the light and show him the watermark, which is that of a Zurich stationer who has never sold a sheet to anyone in Meiringen. He reads it twice, folds it carefully, and puts it in his pocket-book as evidence. 'I am coming to the Falls,' he says. 'Don't argue. I am not a man to be argued with on this subject.'

options.label: Let Watson Go. It Is the Best Way to Keep Him Out of It.
options.detail: He will go to the hotel, find no lady, and be back by dusk. By then the thing will be over.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I shall be an hour, Holmes, perhaps two. If the lady is as ill as the note says, I may be longer. Do not do anything heroic until I am back.

options.outcome: He puts his bag on his shoulder and goes up the lane at a brisk doctorly walk. At the corner he turns, and lifts his hand, and you lift yours. It is the kind of farewell that people make when they are both quite sure of seeing each other at dinner. You stand in the road a long time, and then go the other way.

options.label: Send Him to Interlaken With a Letter for Mycroft.
options.detail: A true errand, and a long one. He will be on the lake steamer by three, and out of the Professor's reach by four.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You have a very unpleasant way of sending a man to the post, Holmes. If you are in any danger, I will not forgive you. If you are not, I shall be insufferable.

options.outcome: You write the letter on the inn's own paper, seal it, and put it in his hand. He reads your face, and you read his, and the thing is settled without a word. He goes down to the steamer with his bag in one hand and the letter in the other, like a man carrying a burning coal. You turn and go up the valley, alone.

options.label: Watson Insists on Coming With You.
options.detail: He will not be sent away, and for once you do not wish to send him. He has earned it.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I know what the note is, Holmes. I can read a forgery as well as you. I am not going to the hotel, and you are not going to the Falls without me, and we shall not discuss it.

options.outcome: He puts the note in his pocket-book, takes his revolver from his bag, loads it in front of you with great deliberation, and puts it in his coat. 'There,' he says. 'Now we may go.' There is nothing at all that you can say, and you do not try.
options.requiresHint: Needs Watson's full trust

options.label: Watson Goes to the Hotel Without Waiting for Your Leave.
options.detail: He does not trust you to tell him the truth, and he has made up his mind to see for himself. You find him gone when you come down.

quote.speaker: The proprietor
quote.text: The doctor has gone up the road, sir, with his bag, a quarter of an hour since. He said you were not to be disturbed. I did think it odd.

options.outcome: The note is on the table, folded small, with a line on the back in Watson's hand: 'I have gone to see. I do not like being managed.' You stand a long moment in the empty room. Then you take your stick, and your hat, and the path.

echoes.text: The thirty pages you wrote last night are in the inside pocket of your coat. You pat them once as you stand there, as a man pats a dog.
Watson knows what you mean to do at the water, and he has been watching your face since breakfast, and is not at all deceived by your manner.

C9.title: The Path Above the Falls
C9.description: Monday 4 May, four in the afternoon. The path to the Falls is a ledge of wet rock, eight feet wide at the widest and three at the narrowest, cut into the mountain above the gorge. On one side is a wall of black stone, glistening with spray. On the other is nothing at all, and three hundred feet down, a boil of white water, with a roar like a battery of guns. A tall figure is coming along the path towards you, swaying. He wears a dark coat and a high hat, and he is quite alone. 'I have come, Mr Holmes,' says Professor Moriarty, 'to finish our conversation.'

options.label: Write a Note for Watson, Then Face Him.
options.detail: Leave a record where he will find it. Then take the Professor's measure, and wait for him to make the first move.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You will allow me the time to write a note? Of course. I have always said that you were a man of method, and I should be sorry to see you fall without it.

success.outcome: You write four lines in your notebook, tear out the page, and weight it with your cigarette-case on the rock. The Professor waits, courteous as ever. Then he comes at you, fast and low, and for a minute and a half there is no sound in the world but breath and the roar of water. His grip is terrible. But you have been trained in the Japanese art of wrestling, and he has not. He goes over.

failure.outcome: You write four lines and leave the case on the rock, and you have time to see that he has already read them upside down. Then he comes at you, with a strength you did not suspect in an old man. You have a hold on his coat as your boots slide on the wet stone, and you do not let go. There is a moment of silence, and then of falling, and then of nothing.

options.label: Hear His Offer a Second Time.
options.detail: The figure he named on the first day is still on the table, and it has grown. It would end everything. It would also end you.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: The figure has increased, Mr Holmes. I had thought to find you altered. I find that I was right. I do not think a man who comes to the edge of a precipice to hear an offer is a man who intends to refuse it.

options.outcome: You stand with your back to the rock and listen, and he names it. It is very large. It is large enough to buy a house in Sussex and a library in London and a quiet mind. You say nothing, and he says nothing, and the Falls thunder on. At the end of a long time you nod, very slightly, and the Professor smiles. It is the first time you have ever seen him do it.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs you to have listened to his offer

options.label: Strike First, on the Narrow Path, Before He Is Ready.
options.detail: The only advantage you possess is surprise. You will have it for exactly as long as it takes to move.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You are a younger man, Mr Holmes, and you are stronger. I wonder if you will find that is enough.

success.outcome: You are across the gap before he has finished speaking, with your left hand at his collar and your right at the back of his knee. It is a trick you have not used since Cambridge. For a moment he hangs, with his hat gone and his white forehead streaming with spray, and then the rock has nothing to hold him. You do not hear the fall. The roar of the Reichenbach takes it.

failure.outcome: He is ready. He has been ready for months. His hand closes on your wrist in a grip like a vice, and you find yourself dragged to the edge by a man older than your father. For one fierce moment you fight, and then the edge crumbles. You hear Watson's name in your own mouth, and then the thunder.

options.label: Take the Fight to the Ledge You Scouted.
options.detail: You know every foot of it. Let him come to you, on the ground you have chosen, and use it.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You have walked this path before, Mr Holmes. I had wondered. It is the sort of care that does one credit, and it will not, I think, save you.

options.outcome: You write your four lines on the rock, as before, and set the case upon them. Then you step back, to the second ledge, and the Professor comes along the path after you in the full spray of the fall, swaying, sure-footed and, for the first time in your acquaintance, very slightly out of breath. You know where every inch of it is. You let him come.
options.requiresHint: Needs the ledge scouted, and a steady nerve

echoes.text: Watson is twenty paces behind you on the path, with his hand in his coat, saying nothing. He has the face of a man who has resolved to be exactly where he is.

C10.title: Moran on the Ridge
C10.description: Monday evening. The Professor is gone, and the path is very quiet. Your hands are shaking, and your coat is torn, and the roar of the water has taken on a hollow, ringing note. You are standing alone on a ledge in the last light when a stone clatters down from the ridge above, and you look up. A tall man is silhouetted against the sky, a hundred feet above, kneeling, with a long, odd-shaped stick across his knee. He raises it to his shoulder. Colonel Moran has seen the Professor fall, and he has a very simple idea of what to do about it.

options.label: Go Down the Cliff in the Dark and Let the World Think You Fell.
options.detail: A ledge, a ledge, and another. You know it from a hundred yards of looking. It is the only way to live, and the long way round.

quote.speaker: Colonel Moran
quote.text: I had hoped, Mr Holmes, to oblige you with something more dignified. But a gentleman must shoot what is in front of him.

success.outcome: You go down hand over hand in the failing light, and a stone strikes the rock above you, and another. A bullet whines off the face, and then there is only the sound of water. You hang in a crack under a ledge for an hour. By the time you come out, Moran has gone, and the night is as black as pitch. There is no one on earth who knows that you are alive.

failure.outcome: The first stone misses. The second does not. The third is not a stone, but a round, soft sound from the ridge, and a blow in the shoulder like the kick of a horse. You hold on for a long moment, and then your fingers open.

options.label: Take the Ledge You Walked With Hans.
options.detail: You know every foot of it from yesterday's dusk. A man who has walked a path in the light may climb it in the dark.

quote.speaker: Hans, the guide
quote.text: Here you put your foot, sir, and here you do not. I told you that. If you remember, you will live. If you forget, I shall be sorry.

options.requiresFlagHint: Needs to have walked the ledge

success.outcome: Your foot finds each hold before your mind has named it: the ledge, the crack, the second ledge below. A stone strikes the rock a yard away, and another, and then there is only the roar of the water and the sound of your own breath. By midnight you are in the hay of a barn above Meiringen, with a bandaged hand, and Hans, who has found you without being told, is saying nothing at all in a most eloquent way.

failure.outcome: You remember the ledge, and the crack, and then you remember that the second ledge is a hand's breadth wider than you thought. The rock goes out from under your boot. You hear a flat, soft sound from the ridge, and a stone that is not a stone, and then nothing.

options.label: Stand With Watson and Answer the Colonel Shot for Shot.
options.detail: Two pistols against one rifle. It is not fair odds, but you have the better reasons.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I am a very indifferent shot, Holmes, but I have a cool head. I shall fire when you fire. We have only to hold him until the guides come.

success.outcome: You fire, and Watson fires, and the Colonel, who has never in his life been shot at by two men at once, flinches. A shot goes wide. A second goes wider. And then the guides' lamps are coming up the valley with a noise of shouting, and Moran swears like a trooper, and is gone. You and Watson sit on the wet rock, side by side, laughing until you are sick.

failure.outcome: The Colonel fires once. It is the only shot he needs. Watson goes down on one knee with a surprised expression, and puts his hand to his side, and looks at it. 'Holmes,' he says, in a perfectly ordinary voice, 'I am afraid I am hit.' You are across the rock in a moment, but you know already how it will end.

options.label: Hold the Professor by the Coat and Go Over With Him.
options.detail: It is not yet over. He is still on the ledge below you, clutching at the rock. The world will be rid of him at the price of you.

quote.speaker: Professor Moriarty
quote.text: You are a fool, Mr Holmes. A very honourable fool. I had not thought it of you.

options.outcome: He is not dead. He is hanging at the end of your arm, with the water roaring under him, and he looks up at you with the clear, curious eyes of a man who has made his last calculation. You do not let go. You lean back, and take him with you. The rock drops away. There is a moment of perfect silence, and a feeling, absurdly, of relief.

options.label: Follow Your Brother's Plan: a Boat Below the Gorge.
options.detail: A rope, a ledge, and a man with a boat on the Aare, paid by Mycroft since Thursday. It is the careful way, and it needs both of you to have thought of it.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: There will be a man at the foot of the gorge with a boat and no questions. I do not ask you to use him. I ask you to remember that he is there.

options.outcome: You go down by the ledge that Hans showed you, hand over hand in the dusk, with the water thundering on the left, and at the foot of the cliff there is, absurdly, a small flat boat with a lantern in it and a Swiss boatman who says nothing at all. He rows you down the Aare in the dark. At midnight you are in a hay-loft above Meiringen with a blanket, and a bottle.
options.requiresHint: Needs the ledge scouted and your brother's trust

options.label: Trust Watson's Aim.
options.detail: He has never missed in a hurry, and he has never been asked to. He is behind you, with his revolver in both hands, and he says that he is ready.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: He is on the ridge, Holmes, to the left of the pine. I have him. I shall fire when you say, and you may be very certain that I shall not miss.

options.outcome: You say the word, and Watson fires, once, with a calm that you have only ever seen in him over an operating table. There is a short cry from the ridge and the soft clatter of a weapon on stone. When the guides' lanterns come up the valley a quarter of an hour later, you are sitting together on the wet rock, laughing like boys.
options.requiresHint: Needs Watson beside you, and his full trust

echoes.text: The four lines you wrote lie under the cigarette-case on the rock, a little yellow square in the dusk. You think of Watson reading them.
Somewhere a mile down the valley, a good man is walking up to a hotel that never had a dying lady in it.

C4B.title: Letters at the Poste Restante
C4B.description: Tuesday 28 April. The poste restante at Brussels is a high, bare, echoing hall with a wooden counter and a clerk who regards the whole of mankind with a mild contempt. There are three letters for 'Mr Henri Dubois'. The first is in a square, honest, policeman's hand, and is four pages long. The second is in pencil, on the back of a handbill, with a great many capital letters. The third is a single sheet of heavy Foreign Office paper, folded very small, and it is the one you do not at once open. You have time to answer one of them before the afternoon train.

options.label: Answer Lestrade at Length.
options.detail: He has written four pages in a hand that cost him an evening. A man who writes like that deserves an answer like that.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I am only a plain man, Mr Holmes, and I do not know what I am to do. But I should like you to know that the Yard is behind you, and that I have told the Chief so.

options.outcome: You write him three pages, in a clear hand, giving him the whole position as you understand it and asking for nothing. It is the first long letter you have written in a year. When you post it, you feel, absurdly, as though you had put a hand on a friend's shoulder.

options.label: Answer Wiggins and Tell Him to Keep the Boys Indoors.
options.detail: The boys do not know what a man like the Professor can do. Someone had better tell them.

quote.speaker: Wiggins
quote.text: DEAR MR HOLMES, ALL THE BOYS ARE WELL. WE HAVE BEEN WATCHING THE HOUSE AND NOBODY HAS COME OUT. MRS HUDSON SAYS YOU ARE TO WRITE. W.

options.outcome: You write on the back of a menu, in plain words, that the boys are to go home and stay there and be good until you return, and you enclose a sovereign for the lot. It is a small thing. But you read the letter once more before you seal it, and you find that you have written 'with my love' without noticing it. You cross it out. Then you put it back.

options.label: Burn the Lot and Move On.
options.detail: A letter is a trail. The fewer links you keep to London, the harder you are to find.

quote.speaker: The clerk
quote.text: Monsieur wishes to burn his letters? Certainly. There is a stove behind the counter. Many gentlemen do. It is very instructive, the things a man will not keep.

options.outcome: The clerk hands you the poker without a word. The three letters burn with a small, clean, yellow light, the Foreign Office paper last of all, and you read the first line of it as it curls. It says: 'He has taken a special. M.' You stand a moment with the poker in your hand. It is not very much to have read, and it is a good deal more than you wished to know.

C5B.title: The Compartment at Basel
C5B.description: Thursday 30 April, the express from Strasbourg to Basel. Watson has gone to sleep in his corner with his hat over his eyes, as a man does who has learned to sleep at any hour on any train, and the compartment is empty but for one other passenger, a stout, pleasant, red-faced German in a green hat who has been looking out of the window for the better part of an hour, and who has, in that time, not once turned a page of his newspaper. He is a very good traveller. He is also holding the paper upside down.

options.label: Talk to Him in German and Learn What You Can.
options.detail: A quiet remark, a pleasant face. Let him think you a harmless Englishman, and listen to what he does not say.

quote.speaker: The German in the green hat
quote.text: You are English, mein Herr? I have a cousin in Manchester. A very large place. They tell me nobody there ever speaks to anybody.

success.outcome: You discuss his cousin, the price of tobacco and the beauties of the Black Forest for forty minutes, and in the course of it he lets fall the name of a hotel in Meiringen that nobody in Basel has any reason to have heard. He gets out at the next station with a perfectly easy smile. You have not caught him. But you know where his master is sending the others.

failure.outcome: He is a good deal cleverer than he looks. Within ten minutes it is he who is asking the questions, so pleasantly that you hardly notice, and in the end you have told him a great many small things about yourself and learned almost nothing about him. He gets out at the next station and tips his green hat to Watson, who is still asleep.

options.label: Wake Watson and Have Him Feign an Attack of Faintness.
options.detail: A doctor has authority. A stranger will give up a seat to a sick man, and the compartment to the man's physician.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You wish me to be ill, Holmes? On a railway train, in front of a foreigner? I have never in my life done anything so undignified. Move your feet, I shall want to lie down.

options.outcome: Watson is magnificent. He sways, he groans, he calls for a window to be opened, and at the end of five minutes the German is on the platform at Mulhouse with a handkerchief to his face, saying something about a connection. 'I trust,' says Watson, sitting up and straightening his hat, 'that I shall never be asked to do that again.' He looks, you think, rather pleased.
options.requiresHint: Needs Watson's trust

options.label: Show Him the Pistol in Your Coat and Say Nothing.
options.detail: No words, no argument. A man in a green hat who has seen a revolver in an English coat will usually find that he has urgent business elsewhere.

quote.speaker: The German in the green hat
quote.text: Ach. I see I have been rude, mein Herr. A man ought not to stare. I shall go and sit with the other gentlemen. It is much more cheerful.

options.outcome: He goes at once, with a polite bow, and a smile which is a little too fixed. You sit for the rest of the journey with your hand in your pocket and your eyes on the door. It is a crude solution. It is also, you reflect, the only one that did not involve you in a conversation.

echoes.text: The black soutane is at the bottom of your trunk, and you wonder, with a certain grim humour, whether a priest would have been asked any questions at all.

C6B.title: The Steamer on the Lake of Thun
C6B.description: Saturday 2 May. The little steamer goes up the lake in the thin spring sunshine, with a ripple of white at her bow and a smell of coal-smoke and fresh water. The snow-peaks stand about the lake like a company of old men at a funeral, and the passengers lean on the rail and say 'ach' and 'oh' and 'ravishing'. For two hours, for the first time since January, nobody is following you. Watson sits on a coil of rope, with his hat tilted over his eyes, and says nothing, and it is the best thing that has happened in three months.

options.label: Tell Him What You Intend if It Comes to the End.
options.detail: A man should not walk into the mountains without a word. If the worst happens, he will want to know that you had a plan.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I see. You think it will end at the water. You will not say so, of course, but you think it. Well. I do not accept it, Holmes. But I thank you for telling me.

options.outcome: You tell him quietly, in the lee of the funnel, that if it comes to the worst there will be a note, and where to look for it. He does not interrupt. When you have finished he puts his hand over yours on the rail, and holds it there for a minute, and says nothing at all. The lake is perfectly beautiful, and neither of you looks at it.

options.label: Ask After Mary, and the Practice, and Let Him Talk.
options.detail: He has put his whole life aside to follow you. Give him an hour of it back.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: She sends her love, Holmes. She said that I was to tell you so, and that you were to eat. I did not like to say it was not a matter I had been able to promise.

options.outcome: He talks for an hour about his wife, and the practice, and the dreadful state of the roof in Kensington, and the new curate who preaches on the subject of drains. You listen with real attention. It is not what you would have chosen to listen to a year ago. It is, you find, extremely restful.

options.label: Watch the Other Passengers for a Face You Know.
options.detail: A lake steamer is a very small stage. If the Colonel is on it, you will see him.

quote.speaker: A Swiss purser
quote.text: You are looking for somebody, monsieur? I have a very good memory for faces. I shall tell you at once that I have seen nobody who is not a tourist or a priest.

success.outcome: You find him at the stern, a tall, lean, sunburnt Englishman in a long coat, with a violin-case under his arm and a book that he is not reading. He does not look at you. He gets off at Spiez, without looking back. You tell Watson nothing. But you watch the shore until the steamer is out of sight of it.

failure.outcome: You see a Colonel in every shadow, and a Professor in every hat, and by the end of the voyage you have frightened a Swiss schoolmaster, a Dutch bride and a very large, very surprised Bishop. Watson takes you by the arm and leads you to a bench. 'You will sit down,' he says kindly, 'and you will look at the mountains.'

C7B.title: The Guide's Warning
C7B.description: Sunday 3 May, in the dusk. The proprietor of the inn at Meiringen has sent for a guide, a leathery old Swiss named Hans who has spent his life on those paths and who talks to you in a slow and patient English like a man reading from a very old book. The path to the Falls, he says, is closed at nightfall, by custom and by common sense. It is cut into the rock, and the spray freezes on it by dark. A man might slip and nobody know. Also, he adds, in the same slow voice, a tall Englishman with a violin-case has asked him the way to the Falls three times today.

options.label: Walk the Path With Him at Dusk and Learn the Ledge.
options.detail: If it comes to a struggle on that rock, the man who knows every foot of it has the advantage. It is a chilly evening's work.

quote.speaker: Hans, the guide
quote.text: Here you put your foot, sir, and here you do not. There is a ledge below, and a crack, and a second ledge below that. I have seen a goat go down it. I have never seen a man.

options.outcome: You walk the whole path in the last of the light, with the roar of the water growing in your ears and the spray cold on your face. Hans points out each place with his stick: the ledge, the crack, the second ledge below. You look at each of them for a long time. You do not say why. He does not ask.

options.label: Send a Coded Telegram to Mycroft.
options.detail: A very short message, saying only where you are. He will know what to do with it, and he will not be pleased to be woken.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Received. Moriarty left Paris on Friday for Geneva. He will be in Meiringen by Monday. I regret that I can do nothing more at this distance. Be careful, and do not do anything noble. M.

options.outcome: The reply comes within the hour, which is, for Mycroft, the speed of an alarm bell. It tells you in nineteen words what you had half-guessed in four days. You tear it up and put the pieces in the stove, and sit looking at the glow. 'Do not do anything noble.' It is the most affectionate thing he has ever said to you.

options.label: Rest. You Will Need Every Ounce of It Tomorrow.
options.detail: A man who goes to a struggle already tired has half lost it. You have not slept properly since Geneva.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: Good, Holmes. I shall sit by the window with my book, and when you start to talk in your sleep I shall make a note. Go on, now.

options.outcome: You sleep for nine hours with Watson in the chair by the window, and when you wake it is bright morning and the smell of coffee is rising up the stair. For ten minutes you lie quite still, looking at the beams of the ceiling, and you do not think about anything at all.

options.label: Hire a Second Guide to Follow the Englishman.
options.detail: A pair of eyes on the stranger, at a franc an hour. It costs a little. It tells you where he sleeps.

quote.speaker: Hans, the guide
quote.text: My nephew is a good boy, sir, and very quiet on his feet. He will follow the gentleman and say nothing, and he will tell you in the morning where the gentleman has slept.

options.outcome: By midnight you know that the tall Englishman has taken a room at the other inn, that he has not undressed, and that he has been out twice to look at the path by lantern. He sits in his window with the lamp turned down. You cannot see his face. But you know the shape of the stick.

H1.title: A Cup of Coffee in Florence
H1.description: Wednesday 6 May 1891. The cafe is in a quiet street behind the Duomo, with a green awning and four small tables, and you have been sitting at one of them for an hour with an English newspaper three days old and a bandage under your glove. It says that you are dead. It says it in a long and handsome obituary, in a black border, with a good many adjectives, and a paragraph on the Professor, who is also said to be dead, and a paragraph on the Falls. You read it twice. There is a great deal in it that is true. It is very strange to be mourned so well.

options.label: Tell No One. Let the World Think It True.
options.detail: A man who is dead is hard to hunt. Every friend you tell is a friend who might be made to speak.

quote.speaker: Your own conscience
quote.text: It is a sound plan, and it is the loneliest that I can think of. I should be very sorry to see you carry it out. I should be a good deal sorrier to see you break it.
