options.outcome: You fold the paper and put it in your pocket. You pay for the coffee, in francs, and go out into the sun with a new name, which is not yet quite your own, and a passport that is entirely your own and entirely false. Nobody in Florence turns to look. It is the most perfect disguise you have ever worn.

options.label: Write to Your Brother, and to Him Alone.
options.detail: Mycroft keeps secrets as a cellar keeps wine. He will send money, and he will tell no one. It is a measured sort of trust.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I have put on mourning, Sherlock. It is very becoming, I am told. I shall send what you ask. I shall say nothing to anyone. I confess I had begun to fear that I should be wearing the black in earnest.

options.outcome: You write four lines in the cipher your family used as boys, and post them in a letter-box in the Via Tornabuoni. Eleven days later a draft arrives at a bank in Florence, in a name you have never used, and a note: 'Do not come home yet.' You laugh, aloud, in the street, for the first time in a month.

options.label: Write to Watson and Risk the Colonel Seeing It.
options.detail: He has been sitting in a dark room, mourning you. A single line would give him back the world. It might also give the Colonel your address.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I have your note, Holmes. I have read it fourteen times. I do not care who is watching me. I should only like you to know that I have never in my life been so glad of a piece of paper.

success.outcome: The letter goes by a Swiss courier and a Parisian bookseller and a Dutch widow who owes Mycroft a favour. It reaches Watson in Kensington on the eleventh day, in a plain envelope, in an unfamiliar hand. He reads it standing up, and puts it into the fire, and then, in a very quiet voice, tells his wife that he will be needing a little extra sleep.

failure.outcome: The letter is opened at a sorting-house in Dover by a clerk who has been paid very well to open a very particular kind of envelope. Within three days a tall, lean, sunburnt man is standing outside a cafe in Florence, looking at the awning. You have gone by then. But you know that you have been found, and that he is a patient man.

H2.title: The Norwegian Explorer
H2.description: Spring 1892. The monastery stands on a spur of rock above a valley that has never been described in English, and the lamas who live in it have never seen a Norwegian, which is exactly what you have decided to be. The air is thin and cold, and very clear, and nothing has happened here for four hundred years. In the morning you walk on the terrace in a sheepskin coat with a notebook, and in the afternoon you sit in a cold cell with a very old monk who is teaching you to be quiet. It is not an art that you have ever practised.

options.label: Study With the Lamas and Learn to Sit Still.
options.detail: A man who can do nothing for an hour can do a great deal more than he could. It is a hard school.

quote.speaker: The old lama
quote.text: You think too much, Sigerson. It is a fault. In this country we call it a disease, and treat it with butter-tea and silence.

options.outcome: For ten months you sit in the cold, and drink butter-tea, and say nothing at all. The old man corrects your posture with a stick. By the spring you can sit for four hours without moving a muscle, and your mind, for the first time since you were a boy, is as still as a pond.

options.label: Send the Foreign Office a Report on the Passes.
options.detail: A traveller sees what a map does not. Your brother would value it, and it would repay the money he has sent.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Your report on the Himalayan passes has been read by three departments and a minister. They are most anxious to know who 'Sigerson' is. I have told them that he is a Norwegian, and that they are not to enquire further.

options.outcome: You spend the summer in the saddle, with a compass and a notebook, and send back a long, exact account of the passes and the garrisons. It is read with attention. In London a very senior man in a very quiet room says that it is the best thing of its kind he has seen. Your name is not on it. Your brother does not tell you what it is worth. You find that you are rather proud.

options.label: Keep to Yourself and Let the Years Pass.
options.detail: You came here to disappear. A man who disappears does not make friends, or notes.

quote.speaker: The old lama
quote.text: You are very polite, Sigerson, and you say nothing. It is a good way to be a ghost. I would not recommend it to anyone I liked.

options.outcome: You keep your cell, your notebook and your own counsel. The monks leave you alone, with the vague, kindly tact of men who have seen a great many people come here to be left alone. When you go down the valley at the end of the year, you realise that you have not said a hundred words aloud since the spring.

echoes.text: A thin, brown-faced Englishman was seen at the foot of the pass in March, asking the way to a Norwegian. He was turned back by the snow. He will not be turned back twice.
At the foot of the pass, in the dusk, a mule driver says that a tall Englishman asked him the way to a Norwegian. He gave a wrong answer, he says, out of habit.

H3.title: The Coal-Tar Laboratory
H3.description: 1893. The laboratory at Montpellier is a long white room with a high ceiling and a row of north windows, and it smells of benzene, hot glass and good cigars. You have been at work there for eight months on the derivatives of coal-tar, under a name that nobody has asked about. It is, you suppose, the happiest period of your life, and you are aware of it as one is aware of a held breath. A letter reaches you in the autumn, forwarded by your brother, in his hand, with four lines. A grievous loss has fallen on Watson. He is not well. He is very much alone.

options.label: Go to Him at Once, Whatever It Costs.
options.detail: A friend in grief cannot be waited for. The Colonel is still at large, and a man who goes home goes home to danger.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I had thought, Holmes, that I should never again hear that step on the stair. I thought it was a dream. I thought that I had lost everything. I find that I was mistaken in at least one particular.

options.outcome: You are in London in thirty-one hours, in a closed cab, in the dark. You sit with him in a silent room until morning, and say very little, and it is, perhaps, the only thing you have ever done that you are wholly sure of. The Colonel does not know. Mycroft, informed by telegram, says only that you are a fool and that he is very glad of it.

options.label: Write Through Your Brother and Stay at Your Work.
options.detail: A letter is a gentle thing, and it can be carried by a man who has no secret to keep. It is not the same as a presence. It is better than nothing.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I shall carry your letter myself. I shall say that it is from a distant friend, a person of great consideration. I do not think he will be deceived. But I think he will be comforted.

options.outcome: Your brother carries the letter, with a face like a funeral, and puts it on Watson's table without a word. Watson reads it twice. He asks who sent it. Your brother says that he cannot say. Watson says, very quietly, that he rather thought so, and folds the paper, and asks whether Mycroft would like some tea.

options.label: Stay. You Cannot Be Seen, and the Work Is Nearly Done.
options.detail: A man who comes out of hiding too soon undoes everything that hiding has done. It is a cold sum, and an accurate one.

quote.speaker: Your own conscience
quote.text: You have always preferred the sum to the answer, and the answer to the man. It has been a long time since I thought it a virtue.

options.outcome: You stay, and you work, and in the spring the monograph is finished. It is a very good piece of research, and it will never carry your name. You have it bound in morocco and put on a shelf. When you look at it, there is, in the corner of your mind, a small, bright, accusing light.

echoes.text: You do not know whether he has the letter you sent from Florence, or whether it was one of the many things that go astray. You only know that a man who has been written to does not grieve in quite the same way.

H4.title: The Return
H4.description: April 1894. The news comes by a London paper two days old, in a cafe in Montpellier: a young gentleman of fashion has been shot dead in a locked room in Park Lane, with a pistol-bullet that nobody can explain. The Yard is baffled. It is, you think, exactly the sort of case that you would have wanted. And you have just learned, from a short note in your brother's hand, that of all the men who ever wished you harm, only one is left alive and at large in London. It is time to decide whether Sherlock Holmes is dead.

options.label: Come Back to Baker Street in a Wig and Spectacles, and Show Yourself to Watson in His Own Study.
options.detail: A theatrical entrance, perhaps. He has had three years of quiet. It may be kinder to be abrupt than to be slow.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I think, Holmes, that I am going to be extremely ill. Please sit down. No, do not be so kind as to explain. I should be obliged if you would simply stand there for a moment, and let me look.

success.outcome: You walk into his study in the dress of an old bookseller with a bag of volumes on his arm, and set them on the table, and say that you are sorry to have startled him. He faints, quite dead away, and falls, with great exactness, into the chair. When he comes round he is crying, and you are on your knees with the brandy. 'You always had a theatrical streak,' he says, and cannot stop laughing.

failure.outcome: It goes wrong at once. The old bookseller's bag falls open, and the volumes scatter, and Watson, who has been up all night, mistakes you for a burglar and has his service revolver out before the second book hits the carpet. You are a long minute explaining who you are, and for the first time in his life Watson is not in the least pleased. It is a long time before you are forgiven.

options.label: Have Mycroft Prepare the Ground, and Return Quietly.
options.detail: A letter first, a visit after, and a cold supper laid in the old rooms. It is a gentle road, and it is slow.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: I have kept the rooms exactly as they were, Sherlock. Mrs Hudson has dusted them every Thursday, and has never once asked why a man who is dead should have his pipes kept filled. She is a remarkable woman.

options.outcome: Mycroft sends a short note to Kensington, which says that a visitor is expected and that the visitor is not to be alarmed. You come in the evening, with your own key, to the old sitting-room. The lamp is lit, and the fire is made, and a cold supper laid for two. Watson, in the armchair, does not turn round. 'Well,' he says, in a perfectly steady voice, 'you took your time.'

options.label: Stay Sigerson. Let the Dead Stay Dead.
options.detail: You have another name, another trade, and a long and peaceful life in front of you. There is not a soul in London who will blame you.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: I always thought, you know, that if it came to it, you would be a man to go very quietly. I did not think it would be quite so thoroughly. I shall go on thinking of you. It will have to be enough.

options.outcome: You put the Park Lane paper down on the table, and finish your coffee, and ask the waiter for the bill. A week later you are in a small house in the south, with a chemical bench and a window on a garden. London has its mystery, and the Yard its bafflement. Somebody else will solve it, in the end, or no one will. You do not read the papers.

echoes.text: You have been to London once already, in the dark, and sat in a silent room until morning. Nobody knows it but Watson, and he has been very careful never to say.

M1.title: The Strangers' Room
M1.description: Saturday 25 April, eleven in the morning. The Diogenes Club is the only place in London where nobody speaks, and the one room in it where talking is permitted is on the first floor, at the back, with the blinds half down. It has a long table, six chairs, a fire that is never allowed to go out, and, tonight, three men. Mycroft sits at the head, vast and unhurried. On his right is the Permanent Secretary of the Home Office, a thin grey man named Aldous. On his left is a man from the Treasury, who has been introduced by his initials. They have been listening to you for twenty minutes. Mycroft has not once looked at the clock.

options.label: Accept the Government's Terms Entire.
options.detail: The machinery of the State at your elbow: Special Branch, the Bank, the Telegraph. In return, whatever you find belongs to the Crown, and goes where the Crown says.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You will find it a great convenience, Sherlock, to have the State at your back. You will also find that it does not like to be asked what it intends. I think you will learn to be content with that.

options.outcome: Aldous makes a note. The man from the Treasury makes a second one. Mycroft folds his hands over his waistcoat and says that the papers will be drawn up by Monday and that in the meantime you may consider yourself a person of consequence. It is a very comfortable feeling. You notice, as you go down the stairs, that your hand has gone to your pocket, as if to make sure that it is still yours.

options.label: Accept, With One Condition: the Law Is Allowed to Run.
options.detail: Use the State's tools, but let the courts have what the courts can use. A reservation, quietly stated, and possibly resented.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: A condition, Sherlock? From you? I had expected something much more extravagant. Very well. Mr Aldous will write it down in a form that allows us all to disregard it at our leisure.

options.outcome: There is a pause, and Aldous looks at Mycroft, and Mycroft looks at the fire. In the end it is written down, in a long and cautious sentence that says nothing and could, in the proper hands, mean a great deal. You are aware that you have bought something. You are not yet sure what.

options.label: Refuse the Terms. Offer Advice, and Nothing More.
options.detail: You will not be a servant of the Crown, however benevolent. You will help, as a private gentleman, and no more.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are very proud, Sherlock. It is a quality I have always rather envied. I shall give you what I can, without terms, and I shall not pretend to be pleased.

options.outcome: Aldous coughs. The man from the Treasury looks at his initials. Mycroft, to everybody's surprise, smiles, very slightly, and says that he had thought as much. He will give you what he can without any paper. It is less than you would have had, and it is clean.

options.label: Wait in the Corridor for an Hour.
options.detail: Your brother has not forgotten how things stood between you. It is a small, cold, very Whitehall way of making the point.

quote.speaker: The hall porter
quote.text: Mr Mycroft will be a little while, sir. He has asked me to say that you are very welcome to sit. He has also asked me to say that there is no hurry.

options.outcome: You sit on a hard chair in a long corridor and look at a portrait of a man who looks like a Lord Chancellor and, you suspect, was. The hour is exactly sixty minutes. When the door opens, Mycroft is behind it with his hands folded, and he says, with a face of perfect blandness, 'Ah. Sherlock. You are early.'

echoes.text: You know the price already. Mycroft named it in February, and has not once mentioned it since, which is how you know that he has not forgotten.

M2.title: Whitehall Wires
M2.description: Saturday, late afternoon. Whitehall in the dusk is a long, grey, hurrying street of lamps and clerks and shuttered windows, and behind every one of them a man is waiting to be told that something is not his department. Mycroft has given you a list of three doors. Behind the first is the Home Secretary's private secretary, who can sign a warrant that no magistrate may question. Behind the second is the Telegraph, which has the Professor's cables in a drawer. Behind the third is the Treasury, which can close an account with a single minute. You have time for one tonight.

options.label: Obtain the Home Secretary's Warrant.
options.detail: A single paper that opens every door in England. It is irregular, and effective, and will be remembered by those who dislike it.

quote.speaker: The Home Secretary's secretary
quote.text: The Secretary has signed it, Mr Holmes, with a very good grace. I should add that he asked me to say that it is not a precedent. I am bound to say that it is a precedent.

options.outcome: The warrant is a single sheet of thick cream paper, with an embossed crest and a signature like a small black bird. You put it in your coat with the faint, unholy feeling of a man who has been handed a loaded gun in a church. It will open every door. It will also close several.

options.label: Read the Professor's Cables at the Telegraph Office.
options.detail: Every word he has sent in six months, in a drawer. It will take all night to read and cost your eyes.

quote.speaker: The chief of the Telegraph
quote.text: They are in cipher, sir. I should warn you that we have never broken it. But I have a young man who has been looking at it for a year, and he says it is not impossible.

success.outcome: By midnight you have the first key, and by four in the morning you have the second, and by dawn you can read a month of the Professor's private correspondence like a Sunday paper. It is cold, courteous, exact and very nearly illegible with malice. You have never in your life been so tired, and so pleased.

failure.outcome: You work all night, and the cipher does not give. At six the young man falls asleep on the table, and you rise with a headache like a hammer and a long, slow, ugly sense of having wasted the Government's time. It is a very small failure. It does not feel small.

options.label: Close the Professor's Accounts at the Treasury.
options.detail: A minute in the right hand, and his bank is told that it cannot pay. It is clean, bloodless and lawful, and it will not be forgotten.

quote.speaker: The man from the Treasury
quote.text: I shall have the instruction sent by messenger in the morning. The Bank of England will be most obliging. It is not often that it is asked to do something it actually wishes to do.

options.outcome: He writes four lines on a Treasury minute-sheet, folds it, seals it, and puts it in a leather case. The whole transaction takes ninety seconds and costs the Professor, you later estimate, a good deal over eleven thousand pounds. It is the most elegant thing that has happened to you since January, and you did not do any of it.

options.label: Let Lestrade Vouch for You.
options.detail: A word from a man the Yard respects. He can do it once. It will mend a good deal, and it will use up what he had.

quote.speaker: Inspector Lestrade
quote.text: I'll say it to the Chief myself, Mr Holmes. I'll say I've known you eleven years. It'll cost me something. I'd as soon you didn't ask what.

options.outcome: Lestrade is gone an hour, and comes back with his collar undone and his hat in his hand. The Chief has agreed, he says, to take another look. The word goes round the building by noon. Doors that were closed are, for the moment, unlocked.

M3.title: The Second Ledger
M3.description: Sunday 26 April. Mycroft takes you down a stone stair in the old part of the building, past three locked doors and a sleeping commissionaire, and into a small bare room with a deal table and a green-shaded lamp. On the table lies a book. It is not the Professor's grey ledger. It is a smaller, older, tattier volume in black American cloth, taken in a raid on a Hatton Garden jeweller six years ago and never returned to the Yard. 'It was meant,' says Mycroft, 'to be burned.' He does not say who decided that it should not be.

options.label: Read It All.
options.detail: Every name, and every page. It will give you the Professor's whole hold on the powerful, and a good deal that a man might prefer not to know.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You will find six members of the Commons in it, Sherlock, and two of the Lords, and a bishop. I did not read it myself. I preferred to have it read to me, by a clerk, with the names left out. It was not the same.

options.outcome: It takes the night. You read the names, and the sums, and the notes in a spidery hand beside each: a debt, a woman, a signature, a Sunday afternoon. By morning you know a great deal about how England is governed, and a good deal more about what it costs. You come up into the grey light of Whitehall with the faint, sick feeling of a man who has read another man's letters.

options.label: Read the First Page and Close the Book.
options.detail: Enough to know what it is. The rest is a weight you need not carry.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are wise, Sherlock. Or you are squeamish. In my experience they come to the same thing, and there is no shame in either.

options.outcome: One page is enough. It lists a dozen names, in a very neat hand, and against each name a sum, and a date, and the single word 'held'. You shut the book. Mycroft nods, with the air of a man who has been spared something, and locks it in a drawer. You do not ask him what he intends. You have the sense that it will be better not to.

options.label: Refuse to Open It.
options.detail: You will not be party to what is in it. A detective's hands should not be in that book.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: As you wish. It will not make it any less true, you understand. It will only mean that I must go on carrying it by myself. I confess that I had hoped for a companion.

options.outcome: You push the book back across the table with one finger. Mycroft does not move for a long moment. Then he takes it, and puts it in his pocket, and says that you may find the way out yourself. You go up the stair alone, and you hear, behind you, the soft heavy sound of a man sitting down.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of a man who has been looked after.

echoes.text: The Home Secretary's warrant is folded in your waistcoat, a small cold square against your ribs.

M4.title: Special Branch
M4.description: Monday 27 April. Superintendent Greaves of Special Branch is a heavy, courteous, silent man with a grey moustache and the dull eye of one who has spent twenty years watching people who did not know they were watched. He sits in the corner of a bare room in Great Scotland Yard with a roll of paper on his knee, and he has thirty men. They are not policemen, quite; they do not wear uniforms, and they do not arrest anyone who is not on a list. He wishes to know, with great politeness, what you would like them to do. He would also like it understood that he does not ask why.

options.label: Strike the Professor's Own House With Special Branch.
options.detail: A quiet, silent, absolutely certain raid, with no newspaper and no inquest. They will take what is there and say nothing to anyone.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Greaves
quote.text: Thirty men, sir, and not one of them will say a word to the press. If there's a paper in the house, we'll have it. If there's a man in it, he'll go to a place that doesn't appear in the books.

success.outcome: The house is taken at three in the morning without a sound. The servants are collected, the doors are locked, and the study is sealed with wax. By dawn there is not a scrap of paper in it that has not gone to a vault in Whitehall. The Professor was not at home. But for the first time his house has been silenced, and the silence is a peculiarly ugly one.

failure.outcome: The house is empty, and has been for three days, and the papers with it. Greaves's men stand about in the dawn with a faintly embarrassed air. It is a perfect, silent, professional failure. It is also, the Professor will see at once, the work of the Government rather than the Yard, and he will know precisely who is behind it.

options.label: Hold Greaves's Men in Reserve.
options.detail: A man in reserve is a man who can be used when it matters. It is slower, and it is wiser.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Greaves
quote.text: In reserve, sir. Very good. I shall keep them where I can find them. A force is like a hat. It is best not to have it out until it is wanted.

options.outcome: Greaves nods, once, with the air of a man who has found a sensible customer. His thirty men go back to the work of looking at people who do not know it. You have lost a day, and kept a weapon. It is not clear which is worth more.

options.label: Ask Greaves What He Really Thinks of the Professor.
options.detail: Twenty years of watching. A man in his position has seen the whole of the case, and has never been asked.

quote.speaker: Superintendent Greaves
quote.text: I think, Mr Holmes, that he's the only man in England who was ever quite sure of himself. It's what makes him dangerous. It's also what'll hang him, if anything does.

options.outcome: Greaves talks for an hour, flatly, in a voice like a man reading an inventory. He has been following the Professor's people for six years, and has never been allowed to touch them. He has a drawer of names and a drawer of dates and a short, dry, unforgiving verdict on every one. When he has finished he asks whether he has been of any use. He has been of the greatest.

echoes.text: Greaves has the Foreign Office clerk's file under his arm. He has the manner of a man who has seen a better coat than his own.
You have met the Superintendent before, at a Club that does not speak. He nods, once, as though it had been a funeral.

M5.title: A Minister's Visit
M5.description: Tuesday 28 April. He comes in a closed carriage, at nine in the evening, and refuses to give his name to Mrs Hudson, who nevertheless knows it. Lord Harcastle is an Under-Secretary of State, a tall, fair, handsome man of fifty with the weary courteous manner of a man who has never been refused anything, and he is plainly frightened. He sits on the edge of your sofa and turns his hat in his hands. He has heard, he says, that there is a book. He has heard that it contains a name. He has come, as a gentleman, to ask whether anything might be done.

options.label: Take What He Knows as a Source, and Spare Him.
options.detail: A frightened man who has seen the inside of the Professor's arrangements is worth a hundred ledgers. Let him buy his safety with what he can tell you.

quote.speaker: Lord Harcastle
quote.text: I will tell you everything I know, Mr Holmes. It is not a great deal, but it is rather more than I should care to see in the newspapers. I trust that I may rely on your discretion.

options.outcome: He talks for two hours, in a low voice, with his hat on his knee. He has dined with the Professor's friends, and lent them his name, and been lent a great deal of money in return. At the end he looks ten years older. You promise nothing. He seems to feel that you have. When he goes, you sit for a long time without moving, with a very odd feeling about the way that things are done.

options.label: Refuse, and Warn Him to Resign.
options.detail: A man in his position can do nothing but go. It is better that he go on his own feet.

quote.speaker: Lord Harcastle
quote.text: You are very hard, Mr Holmes. I had been told that you were a man of reason. I see that I was misinformed. You are a man of principle, and it is a much more uncomfortable thing.

options.outcome: He rises, and puts on his hat, and says that he will think about it. He resigns on Thursday, on the ground of ill-health, and goes to his estate in the north. The newspapers say that it is a pity. You do not. You find, to your surprise, that you do not feel better, only cleaner.

options.label: Hold It Over Him and Take What He Can Give.
options.detail: A man who owes you is a useful man. You will not use it often. You will know that you can.

quote.speaker: Lord Harcastle
quote.text: I perceive, Mr Holmes, that you have chosen your side. I should like to say that I admire it. But I think that you have chosen it very much as the Professor chose his.

options.outcome: He gives you his word, and his word is worth, you suspect, about what you offered for it. You note it in your pocket-book, with a date, in a small neat hand. It is not a pleasant thing to hold. You are aware, putting the book away, of a very small cold sensation, as of a door that has not quite shut.

echoes.text: Greaves's men are in the street outside, in the shadow of the opposite house. Lord Harcastle did not see them. They saw him.
Greaves says, without being asked, that the Colonel has not been seen in London since Friday, and that it is the only thing that has worried him.

M6.title: The Bank's Quiet Room
M6.description: Wednesday 29 April. The Chief Cashier of the Bank of England receives you in a quiet, panelled room with a green carpet, a coal fire and a clock that ticks like a gentleman clearing his throat. He is a small, neat, grey man who has sat in the same chair for thirty years. He has received the Treasury's minute. He would like, he says, to ask what the Government wishes him to do about the Professor's money, which is large, intricate, and, in his considered opinion, not entirely creditable.

options.label: Freeze Every Account at Once.
options.detail: A sudden, total, silent stroke. The Professor's men will be paid nothing, and will notice it by Friday.

quote.speaker: The Chief Cashier
quote.text: Every account, sir? Very good. It will be done by noon. I should add that in thirty years I have never been asked to do so much harm with so little noise.

options.outcome: At noon the Professor's bankers are told, one by one, that their drafts will not be honoured, and by two o'clock the City has heard of it. By four there are seventeen men in London who have not been paid, and who do not know why. The Chief Cashier smiles, for the first time, a small, pleased, dry smile, as of a man who has hit the nail.

options.label: Let a Little Money Flow, and Follow It.
options.detail: A trickle can be traced where a flood cannot. Let him pay his people, and see who is paid.

quote.speaker: The Chief Cashier
quote.text: I can arrange a trickle, Mr Holmes. It will go to eleven accounts at six banks. I should be glad if you would keep a note of them, since I shall be asked to explain it one day.

options.outcome: For three days the Bank's clerks make notes of every payment, to every name, in every currency. By the end of the week you have a map of the Professor's people that no policeman could have drawn. It is a good map. But you have also, you are aware, allowed his men to eat for three days that they would otherwise have starved.

options.label: Leave the Money to the Courts.
options.detail: A freeze is an act of the Crown, and not a verdict. Let the law decide, in its own good time, who is entitled to what.

quote.speaker: The Chief Cashier
quote.text: A very proper view, Mr Holmes. I shall do nothing at all. It is a thing I am very good at, and I assure you that it is a much more difficult thing than it looks.

options.outcome: The Chief Cashier shakes your hand with a gentle, dry, delighted grip. The money stays where it is. In the weeks to come it is the subject of three lawsuits and an inquiry, and the Professor's men are paid in the interim. It is a scrupulous decision, and a slow one, and you cannot quite make yourself believe it is the right one.

options.label: Take a Night at Watson's Fireside.
options.detail: Not a decision, a repair. You can do it once. You will come back to this scene a little less ragged, and a little behind.

quote.speaker: Dr Watson
quote.text: You are to sit in that chair, Holmes, and you are not to speak of the case. Mary has made a pie. I do not propose to argue.

options.outcome: You sleep in the armchair, in your boots, with a rug that smells of lavender over your knees. You wake at dawn with a stiff neck, a clear head, and the faint, foolish feeling of a man who has been looked after.

M7.title: Terms From the Other Side
M7.description: Thursday 30 April. The solicitor comes to the Diogenes Club, which is itself a breach of every rule of the place, and is received by Mycroft in the Strangers' Room with a face as blank as a plate. He is a quiet, pleasant, elderly man named Thorne, who acts for a client who does not give his name. He has a document. It offers, in the most correct and dignified language, to surrender the original of the second ledger and every other paper in the Professor's possession, to leave England within the week, and never to return, in return for an assurance that no proceedings will be taken. Mycroft looks at you. He is, you realise, very much inclined to accept.

options.label: Back Your Brother: Accept the Immunity.
options.detail: The ledger is surrendered, the Professor leaves, and the names are safe. It is not justice. It is the best peace that the State can buy.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are doing the right thing, Sherlock. I know that it does not feel so. It will not feel so for a good many years. But it is the right thing, and I am grateful.

options.outcome: Thorne reads the paper aloud, in a flat dry voice, and Mycroft signs it with a very steady hand. The solicitor folds it, shakes hands all round, and goes away with the air of a man who has done an ordinary morning's business. It is quite quiet in the room for a long time after he has gone. Mycroft pours two glasses of sherry, and you drink yours, and neither of you says what you are thinking.

options.label: Refuse and Press On.
options.detail: The law cannot be bought, even by the Crown. A man who surrenders a ledger will have kept a copy.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: You are making a very great mistake, Sherlock. I do not say that you are wrong. I say that you are making a mistake. There is a difference, and the difference is about nine hundred men.

options.outcome: Thorne rises, folds his paper, and says that he regrets it. Mycroft says nothing at all. For the first time in thirty years you have defied him in front of a stranger, and the stranger has seen it. When the solicitor has gone, your brother turns his chair a quarter-turn to the fire. 'I am not angry,' he says. 'I am merely more tired than I have ever been.'

options.label: Make a Counter-Offer: the Ledger and the Professor.
options.detail: He surrenders the ledger and himself, to a court, in public. A grander and a riskier bargain, and one that he is likely to refuse.

quote.speaker: Mr Thorne
quote.text: I shall carry your reply to my client, Mr Holmes. I should tell you plainly that he does not like to be told what to do. But he has also been known to admire a clever answer.

success.outcome: The reply comes back by midnight, in a very small, very neat, very cold hand: 'Agreed, on one condition. That Mr Sherlock Holmes shall conduct the prosecution himself.' It is the most arrogant paper you have ever read, and you find that you are smiling. You accept it at once, before you can think.

failure.outcome: The reply comes back by midnight, and it is a single line: 'Declined, with regret.' It is signed with a cross. Mycroft reads it over your shoulder and says nothing. You have asked for the moon, and been refused, and your brother knows precisely what it has cost him to stand beside you while you did it.

options.label: Let Mycroft Find a Third Way.
options.detail: He has been looking at it all night. He knows a form of words that is neither the immunity nor the court.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: A closed arrest, Sherlock, and an open trial of the lesser men. The Professor goes to the dock in a month, at a time of my choosing, and the ledger stays in a drawer until it is wanted. It is not a pleasing arrangement. It is the only one that will do.

options.outcome: He lays it out in a quarter of an hour, in a voice like a man reading out a very long and very exact recipe. When he has finished you find that you have no objection to make. It is the neatest piece of work you have ever seen him do, and you are not at all sure that you like what it means.
options.requiresHint: Needs your brother's full trust

M8.title: The Cabinet Room
M8.description: Friday 1 May. The room is on the first floor of a building in Whitehall that does not appear in the guide-books, with a long green table, twelve chairs, and a portrait of the Queen. You sit at the end of it, with your hands on your knees. At the head of the table sits a man you have never met, whose face you have seen in a hundred cartoons, and who has been told, over breakfast, everything that you know. He asks, in a dry quiet voice, what you propose. Mycroft sits at his elbow, looking at the green cloth. Everything has led to this table, and to what you say at it.

options.label: Accept the Crown's Commission.
options.detail: A quiet post, a quiet salary, and every door in England. You will find the Professor's remnants for the Crown, and the Crown will see that nobody ever asks what you did.

quote.speaker: The Prime Minister
quote.text: We should be very glad to have you, Mr Holmes. I will not say that we shall always agree. I will say that I have never yet been bored in the presence of a man who disagrees with me intelligently.

options.outcome: The commission is drawn up on the spot, by a clerk who has evidently done this before. It is a single sheet. It is entirely vague. It says that a Mr Sherlock Holmes of 221B Baker Street is to be given every assistance in the discharge of certain duties of a confidential nature, and it is signed at the foot by three persons, of whom one is your brother. You do not look at him as you sign.

options.label: Take the Second Ledger to the Standard and Publish It.
options.detail: Every name, every sum, every date. The Government will fall. It will deserve to, and so will a good many other things.

quote.speaker: Mr Alderson of the Standard
quote.text: You are quite sure, Mr Holmes? I shall want the whole of it, and I shall print the whole of it. I should say, as a friend, that I have never seen a story that frightened me more.

options.requiresFlagHint: Needs to have read the second ledger

success.outcome: It runs on a Saturday, in eleven columns, without a word cut. By Monday three Members have resigned, a bishop has gone abroad, and the Home Secretary is closeted with the Prime Minister for six hours. By Wednesday the Professor's name is on every tongue in England, and on every lip in the House. It is the most extraordinary week of your life. Nobody can say afterwards that you did the easy thing.

failure.outcome: It runs on a Saturday, in six columns, with the worst of it cut by a nervous sub-editor and the rest denied, in a single sentence, by a Government spokesman. By Monday the story is a rumour, and by Wednesday a scandal about a newspaper. The names are never printed. The Professor, in his quiet room, reads the paper and does not so much as smile.

options.label: Take the Evidence to a Magistrate and Let the Law Run.
options.detail: In the open, with a warrant and a public charge, under the one condition that you made on the first day.

quote.speaker: The Prime Minister
quote.text: I did not think that you would hold to it, Mr Holmes. I confess that I am relieved. It is much easier to be governed by a man who has the courage of his clause.

options.outcome: The Prime Minister, after a very long silence, nods once. Aldous makes a note. Mycroft says nothing, and the corner of his mouth moves, for a quarter of a second, in something that you would have taken for a smile on any other face. The warrant is issued before lunch. By evening the Professor is in a cell in Holloway, and the Cabinet Room has gone back to its ordinary business.
options.requiresFlagHint: Needs the law's condition from the first day

options.label: Let the Professor Go Quietly, Under the Immunity.
options.detail: He surrenders the book and leaves the country. The names are safe. It is the arrangement that your brother wanted, and that you agreed to.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Thank you, Sherlock. I shall not say what it has cost me. I shall say only that I have never in my life been so fond of you, or so frightened of what you might do.

options.outcome: The Professor sails from Southampton on the Tuesday, in a first-class cabin, under his own name, with two trunks and a violin-case. The Cabinet Room goes back to its business. In a locked drawer in Whitehall a small black book lies in the dark. You walk home along the Embankment, by yourself, in the soft grey light, with the gulls going over the river.

options.label: Walk Out of the Room.
options.detail: You will not serve, and you will not publish, and you will not plead. A man may refuse them all.

quote.speaker: Mycroft Holmes
quote.text: Sherlock. Sit down. You are making an exhibition of yourself. Sherlock. Please.

options.outcome: You rise, bow to the Prime Minister, and go out of the room. In the corridor a footman holds your hat. Behind you, through the closed door, you hear a murmur of voices and the soft scrape of a chair. You go down the stair into the sunlight, and into Whitehall, and the Cabinet Room goes on without you.

options.label: Print the Second Ledger With the Editor's Backing.
options.detail: A friend at the Standard, an inspector who will stand behind you in the witness box, and a name or two you can prove. It is not a gamble. It is a campaign.

quote.speaker: Mr Alderson of the Standard
quote.text: I have Lestrade to swear to the chain of custody, Mr Holmes, and a Bishop's chaplain who will swear to the signature. I shall print it as a campaign. If they sue us, they shall have to explain the book.

options.outcome: It runs on a Saturday, in eleven columns, with every name sworn to, and nothing cut. Three Members resign by Monday. By Wednesday the Government has appointed a Commission, and by the end of the summer the Professor's name is the name of an inquiry. It is, everyone agrees, the most complete exposure of its kind in the history of the Press.
options.requiresHint: Needs the ledger read, the Yard's trust and a good name

echoes.text: Lord Harcastle is not at the table. His chair has been moved a very little, and a clerk has been told not to look at it.
You never opened the book. It lies on the green cloth by Mycroft's elbow, black and unmarked, and you do not look at it.

LORE_CITY_MISFORTUNES.headline: A SEASON OF MISFORTUNES IN THE CITY
LORE_CITY_MISFORTUNES.bodyText:
LONDON, Friday. The Lord Mayor's office has received, in the last three weeks, no fewer than forty-one complaints touching irregularities in the discount market, the Lombard Street banks and the Hatton Garden jewellers. Each case, on examination, has proved to be a separate affair. Each has been referred to a separate division of the police. A Cornhill broker, who asked that his name should not be printed, observed that the City was being 'nibbled, sir, as a cheese is nibbled, by a very small mouse that has never once been seen.'

MEANWHILE, in Baker Street, the lamp in a certain first-floor window has been seen burning at four in the morning for six nights together. Neighbours decline to comment.

TRANSITION_YARD.headline: SCOTLAND YARD TO 221B BAKER STREET
TRANSITION_YARD.bodyText: RECEIVED 11.52 P.M. FRIDAY. ASSISTANT COMMISSIONER WILL SEE YOU SATURDAY, TEN O'CLOCK, FIRST FLOOR, LONG ROOM. BRING EVERYTHING. BRING WHATEVER YOU HAVE ON THE PROFESSOR, AND WHATEVER YOU CAN PROVE. THE CHIEF IS SCEPTICAL BUT WILL LISTEN. IF YOU ARE WRONG THIS WILL FINISH US BOTH. LESTRADE.

TRANSITION_STREET.headline: FROM WIGGINS, IN PENCIL
TRANSITION_STREET.bodyText: DEAR MR HOLMES WE HAVE GOT THE MAP DONE. ITS ON THE KITCHEN TABLE. ELEVEN HOUSES AND A DOG. THE BOYS SAY THEY WILL NOT SLEEP TILL ITS FINISHED AND I HAVE TOLD THEM NOT TO BE SILLY BUT THEY WILL. PLEASE COME QUICK. W. WIGGINS. P.S. MRS HUDSON SAYS WILL YOU WIPE YOUR FEET.

TRANSITION_CONTINENT.headline: THE CONTINENTAL EXPRESS: A WARNING TO TRAVELLERS
TRANSITION_CONTINENT.bodyText:
VICTORIA, Saturday. The boat-train for Dover, Calais and the Continent will run as usual this morning, though travellers are advised that the line near Canterbury has been much occupied of late with special trains. The company regrets the inconvenience.

A CORRESPONDENT writes that on Friday evening an elderly gentleman, with a stoop and a broad-brimmed hat, was observed at the Charing Cross Hotel in earnest conversation with a young physician. The gentleman, our correspondent adds, 'was a good deal more cheerful than his years would warrant.'

TRANSITION_REICHENBACH.headline: THE FALLS OF THE REICHENBACH
TRANSITION_REICHENBACH.bodyText: A MILE and a half above Meiringen, the Reichenbach, a stream of considerable volume, descends in a series of leaps into a narrow and exceedingly deep gorge. The best view is obtained from a path cut into the rock above the principal fall, which the traveller will find slippery in wet weather, and in places so narrow that two persons cannot walk abreast. The roar of the water is deafening. Visitors are earnestly requested not to approach the edge.

CRISIS_EVIDENCE.headline: THERE IS NOTHING IN THE FILE
CRISIS_EVIDENCE.bodyText: You read through your own notes for the third time tonight, and the same thing happens that happened the first and the second. Every link in the chain is sound, and not one is proved. A witness has been frightened off. A ledger has been shown to be a copy. A date has been found to be wrong by a day. If you are to take the Professor in a court of law, you will have to find something he cannot explain away, and soon. The case is hanging by a thread, and he knows exactly where the thread is.

CRISIS_STANDING.headline: A GENTLEMAN WHO SEES CONSPIRACIES: THE POLICE GROW WEARY
CRISIS_STANDING.bodyText: A good deal of private irritation has been expressed, in the corridors of Scotland Yard, at the activities of a certain gentleman in Baker Street, who is understood to have a theory of an elaborate criminal conspiracy underlying half the commercial misfortunes of the metropolis. Officers of experience observe that the gentleman has not yet produced a conviction. A senior inspector remarked, 'We are always glad of a clever man. We are less glad when the clever man is wrong, and louder.'

CRISIS_NERVE.headline: FROM A PRIVATE NOTEBOOK, NEVER PUBLISHED
CRISIS_NERVE.bodyText: He has not slept. I have watched him for three nights now, and I do not think he has slept for more than an hour in the stretch. He sits with his knees drawn up and his violin on the floor, and his face has gone the grey of old paper. When I speak to him he turns his head slowly, like a man who has forgotten the way. I know the look. I have seen it in the wards. Someone must make him rest, and I do not think it will be me, because he will not listen.

TRANSITION_MYCROFT.headline: THE DIOGENES CLUB
TRANSITION_MYCROFT.bodyText: MR MYCROFT HOLMES requests the favour of Mr Sherlock Holmes's company at the Club, on Saturday, at eleven in the morning. Mr Holmes will be received in the Strangers' Room, where conversation is permitted. He is requested to arrive punctually, to be brief, and to say nothing that he would not wish to see in the Estimates. The Club regrets that it cannot offer refreshment. It regrets very little else.

TRANSITION_HIATUS.headline: SHERLOCK HOLMES: AN APPRECIATION
TRANSITION_HIATUS.bodyText:
THE news from Switzerland has been received in London with a very general sorrow. Mr Sherlock Holmes, who was understood to have fallen with the notorious Professor Moriarty at the Falls of the Reichenbach on Monday last, was the most remarkable private detective of our time, and, those who knew him will say, among the most remarkable men. He was reserved, brilliant, and, it was sometimes thought, a little cold. It is to be hoped that it will be possible to say, in the years to come, that he was also happy.

His friend and companion, Dr John Watson, has declined to comment.

ENDING_CRISIS_EVIDENCE.title: The Case Collapses
ENDING_CRISIS_EVIDENCE.headline: FAMOUS DETECTIVE'S 'NAPOLEON' CALLED A FANCY: THE PROFESSOR THANKS THE POLICE
ENDING_CRISIS_EVIDENCE.text: It goes slowly, and then all at once. A witness retracts. A ledger is found to be a copy, and the copy a forgery. A bank-book that should have hanged a man is found to be in the wrong year. By the time the Assistant Commissioner closes the file, there is nothing left in it that a jury would look at twice. Professor Moriarty is invited to dine with the Lord Mayor in the autumn, and sends his regrets. You are not invited anywhere. In Baker Street the files lie where you left them, and every one of them is perfectly true, and not one of them can be proved.

variants.headline: WARRANTS QUASHED: THE YARD DROPS THE MORIARTY INQUIRY
variants.text: The warrants are quashed one by one in the week before Whitsun. The magistrate who signs the last of them says, kindly, that he has never doubted your good faith, and Lestrade stands behind you in the corridor, looking at his boots. Eleven addresses were searched. Not one of them is mentioned in the order that closes the file.

variants.headline: A WAR WITHOUT A FILE: NOTHING FOR A COURT
variants.text: There is nothing in the boys' notebooks that a court would hear: a dozen children's pencil-lists, a map in coloured chalk, and a ledger of dates that every barrister in London would call hearsay. The Professor's organisation does not so much as shake. Wiggins asks, once, whether it was all for nothing. You tell him that it was not. It is not a very convincing answer.

variants.headline: THE STATE HAD EVERYTHING BUT A FACT
variants.text: Whitehall has all the power in England and not one fact it can use. Mycroft closes the file with a small, tired movement of the hand. 'We shall have to wait,' he says, 'for him to make a mistake. He has not made one since 1885.' The Cabinet Room is thanked, and dismissed, and the Professor dines out on the Friday.

variants.headline: FROM SWITZERLAND: A CASE LEFT BEHIND IN LONDON
variants.text: You are in a Swiss hotel with a trunk of papers and no case. The telegrams from London say only that the arrests have been released for want of evidence. You read them in silence, one after another, and Watson, across the table, does not ask. The river goes on outside the window, loud and white and entirely unconcerned.

variants.headline: IT NEVER BEGAN: THE FILE ON THE PROFESSOR IS A HEAP OF CUTTINGS
variants.text: It ends before it has properly begun. By April the file is a heap of cuttings and a name nobody will repeat, and the Yard, which never quite opened a door to you, closes it politely. You were right about everything. It is a poor thing to have been, in the circumstances, and a very quiet one.

ENDING_CRISIS_STANDING.title: The Discredited Detective
ENDING_CRISIS_STANDING.headline: BAKER STREET 'CONSULTANT' WARNED BY MAGISTRATE: A MAN WHO SEES CONSPIRACIES
ENDING_CRISIS_STANDING.text: A man may be right a hundred times and wrong once, and the world will remember only the once. By the end of the month there is a paragraph in the Standard, a joke in Punch, a letter from the Home Office and a visit from a quiet gentleman of the Yard. You are told, with every courtesy, that the Metropolitan Police will no longer be requiring your assistance. The clients stop coming. The telegrams stop coming. The Professor, meanwhile, has taken a villa at Sevenoaks and is said to be writing a book. You play the violin, and the street below goes by without looking up.

variants.headline: SCOTLAND YARD: NO FURTHER CONTACT WITH MR HOLMES
variants.text: Lestrade is the last to go. He comes to Baker Street on a wet evening in May to say, very awkwardly, that the Chief has forbidden further contact, and that he has never in his life been so ashamed of an order. He does not stay for tea. At the door he turns and says that he, for one, never doubted a word. It is the kindest thing anyone says to you that year.

variants.headline: A GENTLEMAN WITH AN ARMY OF CHILDREN: THE YARD TAKES NOTICE
variants.text: The Yard decides, at last, that a gentleman who commands an army of street children is a gentleman to be watched. Two constables are posted at the corner of Baker Street. They are, you realise, not there to protect you. Wiggins and the boys are not seen again at the area door, and nobody tells you where they have gone, and you do not ask.

variants.headline: WHITEHALL FORGETS
variants.text: Whitehall forgets you with an elegance that is almost beautiful. The doors do not shut. They simply cease to be there. At the Diogenes Club a servant tells you, in a very low voice, that Mr Mycroft is from home, and has been for some time. You stand on the steps in the rain, a man who was, a month ago, a person of consequence.

variants.headline: 'HOLMES FLEES': THE PAPERS HAVE IT AT LAST
variants.text: The London papers have found you out. 'HOLMES FLEES', says the Standard, in an inch of black type, and the Professor's friends supply the rest. You are a fugitive from your own reputation, in a foreign hotel, with a revolver and a friend. Watson reads the paper aloud to you in a flat, steady voice, and when he has finished he folds it, and says that he has never believed a word.

variants.headline: A WORD, A PARAGRAPH, A POLITE REFUSAL
variants.text: It does not take long. A paragraph, a rumour, a polite refusal at the Yard. By Easter the notes on the mantelpiece have stopped coming, and Mrs Hudson has begun to dust the pipe-rack with the air of a woman clearing a room for a funeral. You are the cleverest man in London, and nobody wants to hear it.

ENDING_CRISIS_NERVE.title: The Black Dog
ENDING_CRISIS_NERVE.headline: CELEBRATED DETECTIVE TAKEN ILL: DOCTOR FORBIDS ALL VISITORS
ENDING_CRISIS_NERVE.text: There is a limit to what a mind can do without sleep, and you have been past it since March. It comes in the small hours, in a silence so total that you hear the blood in your ears: a heaviness, a sullen refusal of the machine to turn. You sit in the chair and cannot rise. Watson comes at dawn with his bag and his grave, tired face, and sits with you through the morning, and says nothing that is not kind. The Professor has won nothing. He has only waited. A man who has driven himself so hard, you understand, needs no enemy in the end.

variants.headline: ON THE MORNING OF THE RAIDS: A GREAT DETECTIVE TAKEN ILL
variants.text: It comes on the morning of the raids. You stand at the long table at Scotland Yard with eleven warrants in front of you and cannot read the first of them. Lestrade takes you by the elbow, very gently, and says that he will see to it. He does see to it. The raids go forward, and the net closes, and you are not there to see it.

variants.headline: THE BOYS TAKE OVER: A CELLAR IN LISSON GROVE
variants.text: The boys find you in the cellar of the Lisson Grove lodging, sitting on an upturned crate with a candle and your hands in your lap. Wiggins takes off his cap. 'Mr Holmes,' he says, very low. 'Mr Holmes. We'll take it from here.' They carry you up the stair between them, five small figures and one tall one, with a great deal of whispering.

variants.headline: A VAST PATIENT FIGURE BY THE WINDOW
variants.text: Mycroft finds you on the steps of the Treasury at four in the morning. He does not ask. He takes you home in a closed carriage, puts you to bed, and for three days sits in the chair by the window, a vast patient figure, reading the Gazette. When you wake he says only that he has cancelled the Cabinet, and that you are not to be thanked for it.

variants.headline: A HOTEL IN GENEVA: A DOCTOR WRITES TO LONDON
variants.text: In the Geneva hotel you wake in the dark and cannot remember the name of the town. Watson, in the next room, hears you speaking to the wall. He sits with you until the morning, and then he writes, in cipher, to your brother. The Falls are three days off. You will not see them.

variants.headline: AN ARMCHAIR, A MORNING, A CAB
variants.text: It is not dramatic. You simply cannot get out of the chair. Watson finds you at nine, grey and silent among the papers, and sends Mrs Hudson for a cab. The case, which you had thought so large, turns out to have been a great deal smaller than the man who was trying to carry it.

ENDING_NET_CLOSES.title: The Net Closes
ENDING_NET_CLOSES.headline: NAPOLEON OF CRIME TAKEN AT LAST: PROFESSOR MORIARTY IN CUSTODY
ENDING_NET_CLOSES.text: The trial at the Old Bailey lasts eleven days. Professor Moriarty stands in the dock with his hands folded, a tall, patient, scholarly figure, and listens to the whole of it with the attentive politeness of a man at a lecture. When the verdict is read he inclines his head, as if to a colleague whose argument he had expected. The sentence is penal servitude for life. In the weeks that follow, the network that took ten years to build falls into pieces, and a hundred small crimes across London simply stop. Lestrade shakes your hand on the steps of the court. 'I'll not say I understood it,' he says. 'But I'll say it was done right.'

variants.headline: THE LAW AT LAST: A CLAUSE KEPT
variants.text: The trial is held in public, at the Old Bailey, in the first week of June, because you insisted on a clause and your brother, who has never in his life been outflanked, was outflanked. The Professor stands in the dock with his hands folded and his head swaying slowly from side to side, and he listens to every word of it as if it were a lecture. The Government sits on its hands in the gallery, and very nearly all of it is spared. It is the cleanest victory of your career, and you feel not the least inclined to enjoy it.

variants.headline: TWELVE BOYS ON THE ROOFS: THE NET CLOSES
variants.text: The Professor is taken on the towpath at three in the morning with a carpet-bag in his hand, and it is the boys who saw him first, twelve small whistles passed from slate to slate down the length of the street. Wiggins is thanked in the Commissioner's own office, in a clean collar. He tells the story for the rest of his life, with the twelve boys, and the whistles, and the Commissioner's handshake, and he never once says that he was frightened.

variants.headline: A SINGLE DOOR, A SINGLE GUESS
variants.text: You staked everything on the canal, and the Professor came by the canal, as he had to, a long figure on the towpath with a bag in his hand. Lestrade says afterwards that it was the finest piece of work he ever saw and the most reckless, and that he does not want to see either again. You say that it was not a guess. He says that it was. You both leave it at that.

variants.headline: THE LAW HAS ITS DAY: NO BARGAIN WITH THE PROFESSOR
variants.text: The trial lasts eleven days, and it is held in public, to the last witness, because you refused your brother's quiet arrangement. The names in the Professor's second ledger are read out in open court, and two Members of Parliament resign before the week is out. The Government is furious. The press is rapturous. You receive a short note from Mycroft, written in a hand that is noticeably less steady than usual. It says only: 'You were right, and I shall never forgive you.' The Professor goes down for life, and so, in due course, do eleven men of rank.

variants.headline: A TRAITOR IN THE YARD AND A NAPOLEON IN THE DOCK
variants.text: The trial lasts eleven days. The Professor is convicted, and so is Sergeant Pike, who sells the Yard's secrets in the same dock. The Yard is ashamed and grateful in about equal measure, and the shame lasts longer. Lestrade is made Chief Inspector. You are asked to dinner by people who would not have asked you in January. It is a victory that leaves a taste in the mouth: the net is closed, and a good many hands have been burned by it.

variants.headline: A QUIET WORD IN WHITEHALL, AND THE NET CLOSES
variants.text: The trial lasts eleven days, and it runs more smoothly than a trial of its kind has any right to. Doors open. Witnesses arrive. A file that was lost is found again. You know whom to thank, and you know that one day you will be asked to return the favour. The Professor is sentenced to penal servitude for life, and Lestrade shakes your hand on the court steps, and does not ask why the road was so clear.

ENDING_NAPOLEON_ESCAPES.title: The Napoleon Escapes
ENDING_NAPOLEON_ESCAPES.headline: GREAT ROUND-UP AT SCOTLAND YARD: PRINCIPAL STILL AT LARGE
ENDING_NAPOLEON_ESCAPES.text: The gang is broken, and the Professor is not. The newspapers print the numbers: thirty-one arrested, nineteen convicted, a bishop's secretary in the dock. Of the man whose organisation it was, they print only a name, and a question. He is believed to have left England. He is believed to be in Lisbon, or Vienna, or Buenos Aires. He is believed, by the more imaginative papers, to have died. You know better. Somewhere there is a mild, tall man in a quiet room who has begun again. The war is not over. It has only changed address, and you will have to follow it.

variants.headline: A MAN WHO WOULD NOT BE A SERVANT, OR A WITNESS
variants.text: You walk out of Whitehall into the sunlight, and the Professor goes on, quietly, as he has always done. The Cabinet makes its arrangements without you. The names in the black book are not printed, and not burned, and not forgotten. Mycroft, in his office, takes off his spectacles and rubs the bridge of his nose and says to nobody at all that he had not thought you would do it. It is a very quiet end to a very noisy year.

variants.headline: THE WAR ENDS WITHOUT AN END
variants.text: The Professor goes down the river in the dark, and you let him, and walk the length of Narrow Street with Alf's name in your head. You have not won, and you have not been beaten, and there is a boy in a grave at Limehouse to tell you that it was not a game. Wiggins does not speak to you for a month. When he does, he asks only, in a very small voice, whether it was worth it. You tell him that you do not know. It is the first true thing you have said to him in a year.

variants.headline: THE NET WAS DRAWN. THE FISH WERE NOT ALL IN IT
variants.text: The lieutenants go to prison for ten years, fifteen years, life. The Professor goes nowhere at all. The Yard's inquiries lead to Calais, then to Marseilles, then into a long, grey silence. Lestrade says it was a fine piece of work. You say that it was half a piece of work. You are both right. The Professor's chair stands empty in his study at Kensington, with the chess game unfinished, and black to move.

variants.headline: A BROTHER WHO KNEW WHERE
variants.text: The Professor leaves England by a route that the Yard never finds. Mycroft finds it for you, and sends a single line on Foreign Office paper: 'He sailed from Antwerp on Tuesday. I thought you should know. I did not think you should do anything about it.' You keep the note in the drawer with the ledger. The war goes on, but it goes on at a distance, and your brother is now a party to it.

ENDING_REASON_OF_STATE.title: Reason of State
ENDING_REASON_OF_STATE.headline: PROFESSOR MORIARTY: A SEALED PROCEEDING AT THE OLD BAILEY
ENDING_REASON_OF_STATE.text: He is never tried in public. A closed court is convened by a judge whose name is not in the paper, in a room that does not appear on any plan of the building, and when it rises, the Professor is gone. Some say he is in Dartmoor under another name. Some say he is a guest of the Government in a house in the country. No one says that he is free, and no one says that he is not. The Prime Minister thanks you in a private letter for your discretion. Mycroft sends a case of claret. You drink none of it. Somewhere, in a locked drawer in Whitehall, a grey cloth ledger lies in the dark, and a good many men sleep a little easier.

variants.headline: SOUTHAMPTON, TUESDAY: A GENTLEMAN SAILS
variants.text: He sails on the Tuesday, in a first-class cabin, under his own name, with two trunks and a violin-case, and the newspapers say nothing, because no newspaper has been told. The names in the black book are safe, and the House of Commons sleeps quietly. Mycroft sends a case of claret, which you give to Mrs Hudson, who gives it, in turn, to the milkman. It is the nearest thing to a joke that the whole of the Moriarty business has produced.

variants.headline: THE GOVERNMENT CLOSES ITS OWN LEDGER
variants.text: You know what is in the second ledger, because Mycroft told you. You know who is in it, and why they are not in the dock. The knowledge sits in you like a cold stone. The Professor has been disposed of with every propriety, and a nation's secrets have been kept, and your brother has never in his life been so pleased with you. You wonder, in the small hours, whether you have served the law or merely the men who write it.

ENDING_PRIVATE_WAR.title: The Private War
ENDING_PRIVATE_WAR.headline: MYSTERY OF THE LIMEHOUSE WHARF: BODY OF A TALL MAN TAKEN FROM THE THAMES
ENDING_PRIVATE_WAR.text: They find him on the second morning, caught in the piles at Limehouse, and the coroner records an open verdict. There is nothing to connect the drowned man with the Professor except the shape of his forehead and the fact that, within a month, the great grey organisation of the City is in ruins. Banks close their doors. Lieutenants turn on each other. The cab-yards, the printing-shops and the public-houses are quiet. London does not know who did it. The Yard has a suspicion, and does not trouble to pursue it. You have won the war, in your own way, and the only decoration you will receive is the silence of men who prefer not to ask.

variants.headline: A WAR WON, A BOY LOST
variants.text: They find the Professor on the second morning, and a month later they find nothing at all left of his organisation. Wiggins comes to Baker Street in his best coat, and stands in the sitting-room with his cap in his hands. 'It was worth it, wasn't it, Mr Holmes?' he says. You say yes. It is the only lie you have ever told him, and he knows it, and he thanks you for it. The boys never speak of Alf. They carry on, and are very quiet.

variants.headline: THE IRREGULARS' VICTORY
variants.text: They find the Professor on the second morning, and a month later the whole of his organisation has dissolved like sugar in water. The Irregulars have a party, in the kitchen at Baker Street, with a ham and a cake and a barrel of ginger-beer. Alf, with his arm in a sling, makes a speech that nobody can hear for cheering. Wiggins makes you stand on a chair. You have never in your life been so embarrassed, or so happy.

variants.headline: NO ONE ASKED HOW
variants.text: The Professor is gone, and the Yard is relieved, and nobody mentions the Shoreditch counting-house or the cab-yard or the printer's shop. Lestrade comes to Baker Street, accepts a whisky, and says only that if there should be any more unfortunate accidents of the sort, it would be a kindness if the gentleman responsible would let him know in advance. You promise that there will be none. It is a promise you mean. It is also, you think, the last one you are sure of.

ENDING_BAKER_STREET_BURNS.title: Ashes in Baker Street
ENDING_BAKER_STREET_BURNS.headline: FIRE IN BAKER STREET: FAMOUS LODGINGS DESTROYED; THE PROFESSOR UNSEEN
ENDING_BAKER_STREET_BURNS.text: You are fished out at Wapping Stairs by a lighterman who takes you for a drowned seaman, and carried to a lodging-house with a cup of tea and a blanket. The house in Baker Street is a charred shell by the time you reach it. The papers are ash. The violin is a few burnt strings in the cellar. Of the Professor's organisation, the newspapers report that it has survived the police, the Yard and the Shadow War, and has emerged, if anything, stronger. London goes about its business. You stand in the wet street with Watson, and look up at the black, empty windows, and begin to think about what it is that you have left to lose.

variants.headline: BAKER STREET LOST. MRS HUDSON SAFE IN BRIGHTON
variants.text: The house is gone, and the Professor is not, and there is only one thing to be thankful for: Mrs Hudson, who is a hundred miles away in Brighton with a hamper and a cold. She comes up on the first train, in her black bonnet, and stands in the road with her hands folded. 'Seventeen steps, I counted them every morning,' she says, in a voice that is not at all steady. 'Well. They're gone now. Come along to Brighton, the pair of you, and have a decent breakfast.'

ENDING_THE_COMPACT.title: The Professor's Terms
ENDING_THE_COMPACT.headline: SOCIETY NOTES: A CELEBRATED CONSULTANT RETIRES TO THE COUNTRY
ENDING_THE_COMPACT.text: It is a very handsome house, with a library and a long garden that runs down to a stream, and you are told that the money will come from a bank in Zurich. You are not told which bank. You are never asked to do anything. You are simply asked to stop, and the Professor's people, whom you pass sometimes in the lane, tip their hats with exactly the right degree of courtesy. London goes on being what it is, a little quieter, a little richer, a little more afraid. You read in the papers that a clerk has been found drowned. You turn the page. In a locked drawer you keep the grey ledger, which you have never opened again.

variants.headline: A SWISS HOLIDAY: THE DETECTIVE RETURNS ALONE
variants.text: You come down from the Falls with the Professor's paper in your coat, and a very different idea of what you are. Watson never learns what passed on the path. He is told only that the Professor was not there, and that you changed your mind. You go to Interlaken. In the autumn, a house in Sussex is bought in a name that is not yours. You do not ask where the money came from, and you do not much like the look of your own face in the shaving-glass.

ENDING_THE_FALL.title: The Reichenbach Fall
ENDING_THE_FALL.headline: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT IN THE SWISS ALPS: TWO ENGLISHMEN FEARED LOST AT THE REICHENBACH FALLS
ENDING_THE_FALL.text: The guides search the gorge for three days, and find nothing. At the edge of the path above the Falls, in a patch of trodden mud, there are two sets of footprints that go to the brink and none that come back. A walking-stick leans against the rock, with a cigarette-case beneath it. In the English papers the obituary of Sherlock Holmes is a long one, and kind, and in some places wrong. The Professor's name is printed beside yours. In a village in the valley, for many years afterwards, they will point out the place to travellers, and say that two men met there, and that only the water knows what they said.

variants.headline: A LETTER FOUND ON THE PATH: DR WATSON'S LAST DUTY
variants.text: Watson finds the note at dusk, after the hotel and the empty bed and the cold evening walk back along the river. It is four lines long, folded under your case. He reads it twice by lantern-light. He sits down on the wet rock, and stays there until the guides come at midnight to take him away. In the years after, he writes the whole thing out in a clear, grave hand, and calls it the Final Problem, and does not once say what he thinks of the man who sent him to the hotel.

variants.headline: TWO ENGLISHMEN AT THE FALLS: ONE SURVIVOR
variants.text: Watson was beside you on the path, and he was the one who saw it. He tells the guides, in a flat voice, that the Professor came along the ledge, that there was a struggle, that the two men fell together. He does not say what you said before. He puts your note in his pocket-book, and carries it for the rest of his life, and when he is asked, years afterwards, whether he has ever lost a friend, he answers only that he has lost the best and the wisest man whom he has ever known.

variants.headline: A BROTHER IN BLACK
variants.text: Mycroft is told by telegram, and arrives in Meiringen on the fourth day, in a closed carriage, a great grey presence at the edge of the gorge. He says nothing at all. He looks at the water for a long while, and then at the stick, and then he asks the guides, courteously, to leave him alone. When Watson finds him he is sitting on the wet rock with his hat in his hands. It is the only time that anyone has seen the elder Holmes brother without his composure.

ENDING_THE_EMPTY_GRAVE.title: The Empty Grave
ENDING_THE_EMPTY_GRAVE.headline: HOLMES: A MEMORIAL. THE GREAT DETECTIVE'S NAME REMAINS IN BLACK
ENDING_THE_EMPTY_GRAVE.text: You decide that the dead shall stay dead. In the house in the south of France there is a chemical bench, a window on a garden, and a very good view of the sea, and nobody comes to it who has any idea who you have been. The Park Lane mystery is solved by somebody else, or by nobody. The Professor's organisation is a ruin, and the Colonel is a hunted man. London goes on without Sherlock Holmes, quite as well as it did with him, and rather more quietly. In the evenings you play the violin, to the window, and the window does not applaud.

variants.headline: ONE MAN WHO NEVER KNEW
variants.text: You told no one at all, at the beginning, and you have kept to it. There is not a person alive who has your address. The silence has grown round you year by year, like a coat of dust on a shelf, and it has become a kind of comfort and a kind of cell. Sometimes, in the dusk, you think of Watson, and then you do not.

variants.headline: ONE MAN IN LONDON KNOWS
variants.text: Your brother's draft arrives every quarter, with a short note that says nothing. He knows where you are, and he has kept it from every living soul, including the Prime Minister. He writes in the cipher of your boyhood, and sometimes, at the foot, he writes the name of a book that he thinks you ought to read. You do not tell him that you would sooner he came to see you. It is not a thing that you say.

variants.headline: A FRIEND'S FUNERAL
variants.text: Watson came back from the hotel at the Falls and found the note, and the cigarette-case, and the stick. He did not know what to believe, so he believed the worst. You know it, and you have not written. It is a thing you tell yourself you will put right, in the spring. In the spring you tell yourself that it will be the next one.

ENDING_WATSON_STANDS.title: Two at the Falls
ENDING_WATSON_STANDS.headline: REICHENBACH TRAGEDY: THE PROFESSOR DEAD, THE DETECTIVE SAFE. COLONEL MORAN FLEES
ENDING_WATSON_STANDS.text: The guides arrive with their lanterns just after dark, and find two Englishmen sitting on a wet rock with a revolver between them. The Professor's body is found two days later at the foot of the Falls. Colonel Moran has been taken at Interlaken, in a railway carriage, with an air-gun in a violin case. In Baker Street, a month afterwards, the lamp is lit and the fire is kept, and the old armchair across the hearth is occupied again. Watson writes it all down, in his own way, and gives it to a magazine. You tell him that it is too romantic. He tells you that you are an ungrateful man. It is, you both agree, a perfectly satisfactory way to end an argument.

variants.headline: THE CASE-BOOK AND THE CARRIED LETTER
variants.text: The thirty pages you wrote at the inn are never needed. You carry them back to London in your breast-pocket and give them to Mycroft, who files them without reading, and says that it is a pity to waste such good work. Watson reads them in a night, in the old armchair, and sets them down with a face you have not seen before. 'You were prepared to die,' he says. 'You wrote it all down in case.' You tell him that you were prepared for anything. It is almost the truth.

ENDING_FATAL_SHOT.title: The Colonel's Shot
ENDING_FATAL_SHOT.headline: ENGLISH DOCTOR SHOT DEAD AT THE REICHENBACH FALLS: AIR-GUN SUSPECTED
ENDING_FATAL_SHOT.text: The report of an air-gun is very small, and is lost entirely in the roar of the water. The guides, who come up with their lanterns in the early dark, find no struggle and no robbery, only a body on a rock and a living man sitting beside it, not speaking. The Professor lies at the foot of the Falls. The Colonel is taken at Interlaken three days later, quietly, in a railway carriage. It is no consolation. The war is won, and a friend is dead, and the long ride home in a first-class carriage is the quietest you have ever known.

variants.headline: DR JOHN WATSON: A SOLDIER'S DEATH
variants.text: Watson dies on the ledge, with his hand in yours, saying something about a patient in Kensington whom he has forgotten to see. It is a small, absurd, ordinary last remark, and you will remember it for the rest of your life. Mary Watson is told in London by Mycroft, who takes the news in person. You go back to Baker Street by yourself. The armchair across the hearth is the first thing you see when you light the lamp. You do not sit in your own for a very long time.

variants.headline: HOLMES SHOT ON THE SWISS PATH
variants.text: You die on the ledge alone, with the last light going out of the sky and the thunder of the Falls in your ears. Watson, summoned by a false message to an empty hotel, comes up the path at nightfall and finds you gone. In a notebook, under the rock, there are four lines in your hand. He reads them. He sits down in the road. He does not get up for a long time. The world believes that the greatest detective in London met his death in a fight with the Napoleon of crime. It is, as these things go, very nearly the truth.

ENDING_THE_RETURN.title: The Return to Baker Street
ENDING_THE_RETURN.headline: MR SHERLOCK HOLMES ALIVE: THE GREAT DETECTIVE RETURNS AFTER THREE YEARS
ENDING_THE_RETURN.text: The Park Lane mystery is solved within the week, and the world, which had stopped expecting anything of the sort, takes the news with a gasp. There is a long, loud, delighted correspondence in the newspapers. The Yard sends a polite note. A man who had been buried in a black border is sitting, in the same armchair, with the same pipe, in the same cloud of smoke, as if the Reichenbach Falls had been a fortnight's holiday. Mrs Hudson, on being told, puts her apron over her head and goes into the pantry, and comes out again looking very well. The rooms smell, for a month, of lavender and old books.

variants.headline: A BOOKSELLER'S SURPRISE: DR WATSON FAINTS IN HIS STUDY
variants.text: Watson tells the story of that afternoon, afterwards, to anyone who will listen, and at each telling it grows a little. He had been writing at his desk when an old bookseller came in with an armful of volumes, and the bookseller had said something about a bargain, and when he looked up the bookseller was gone and in his place was a lean, pale, grinning, perfectly familiar face. 'I have never fainted in my life,' he says. 'I fainted then. And I'll thank you not to laugh.' You do not. Not very much.

variants.headline: THE LAMP LIT AND THE SUPPER LAID
variants.text: You come in with your own key, by the old stair, to the room that has not changed. Watson is in the armchair. He does not turn round.
